speechtext: I take it that what in fact was sought was unanimous consent to go to the presentation of reports.

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mrs. McDougall that Bill C-79, an Act respecting the provision of compensation to depositors of Canadian Commercial Bank, CCB Mortgage Investment Corporation and Northland Bank in respect of uninsured deposits, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee; and the amendment of Mr. Turner (Vancouver Quadra) (p. 7379).

Just before the adjournment of the House yesterday, Mr. Speaker, 1 was saying that the purpose of this Bill is to refund uninsured deposits, meaning those exceeding the $60,000 insurable limit. According to the Government, people who in good faith deposited their money with the Canadian Commercial Bank because they relied on Government guarantees should not be penalized.
Mr. Speaker, did the Government give guarantees? If so, why does it not tell the House about them? Since Canadian taxpayers will have to repay the depositors, our responsibility towards those taxpayers is to find out who will get the money. The Bill provides that depositors must file an application to get their money back, so we can expect to know who they are, sooner or later. Therefore, since we are being asked to adopt the Bill now, it is quite reasonable that we should be given that information right away.
Passage of this Bill will cost the Canadian taxpayers nearly $1 billion. This is a very large amount especially for a Government which pretends to be money concious and which says that it cannot afford to pay family allowances or to maintain social housing, energy, investment of environmental programs, and the list goes on.
Mr. Speaker, last spring, while we were discussing the bail out of this bank, we also amended the Small Businesses Loans Act. In that case also, changes were made because the Government could not afford certain loans. Now, the small businessman must pay 1 per cent on his small business loan and provide an 85 per cent guarantee while the Government used to provide a 100 per cent guarantee.
Now, the Government is asking us to provide full reimbursement, or a 100 per cent guarantee, to these depositors whose names we do not even know.

October 10, 1985
Depositors Compensation

The fact is that we have seen the failutre of two western banks which were accredited to the international sphere as being sound and viable institutions in the financial forum. To see their lose credibility face is rather upsetting for everyone involved, especially the depositors who are questioning the return of their deposits. Today, we are being asked by the governing Party to agree to a Bill without having all the information before us. I must say that we will not fall into a blind-eye policy. It is evident that the unsecured depositors must apply in order to receive reimbursement; so why tell us who they are? Is the Government trying to hide something? Is there some type of cover-up?
On March 25, 1985, the Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDougall) said in the House, and I quote:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to advise the House that an agreement was reached this morning to provide the Canadian Commercial Bank with an infusion of capital which will ensure the long-term viability of this Edmonton-based bank. The agreement is a co-operative effort which brings together three Governments, six banks, and the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation to provide a support package which will enable this bank to remain viable, thereby protecting the interests of small and medium-sized business in western Canada.
What happened six months later? This bank was supposed to be viable after the pouring into it of S250 million. [Translation]
On March 28, 1985, the same Minister stated in this House:
Our concern as the federal Government must also extend beyond western Canada. We want to make sure that a ripple in the financial system does not spread from coast to coast and beyond, to overseas markets. The Government must also be concerned with the effect a failure might have on the stability, security and confidence of the entire financial system.
Mr. Speaker, since the summer of 1984, the Progressive Conservative Party has been repeating that we need confidence! Yet, one year later, what kind of confidence is there? Two banks have gone bankrupt.
Once more, I quote the Minister, who said:
By addressing the present matter quickly, we are guarding against a potential erosion of confidence in our financial system both at home and abroad. This decisive action is evidence that our financial institutions are safe for depositors.
Now, six months later, it is no longer safe for depositors, and to save face the Government is asking us to reimburse the depositors without giving us the names of those who are owed all this money.
The question all Canadians are asking today is this: Why does the Government not want to provide names? I would like to conclude my comments by saying that the Government might say that it is to protect banking confidentiality, but this matter is no longer confidential as the bank has gone bankrupt. When you go bankrupt, you have to give all the names. I shall therefore vote against this Bill because the Government does not want to provide us with names.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The Hon. Member for Beaches.
It is Winnipeg North Centre, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Excuse me, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North Centre.

Mr. Speaker, I would be a bit disturbed with respect to being transferred to a riding in Toronto. At any rate, it is a pleasure to be able to enter into this debate under whatever designation. We only have a short time to contribute to this debate, Mr. Speaker, but there are significant points which need to be made. First, I think the public's attention with regard to this legislation to bail out these banks must be focused on the hearings which are going on right now and the press reports which are beginning to emerge.

For example, there was an analysis in The Globe and Mail today with regard to the Hitchman Report. The facts are coming out now with regard to the condition of the bank when the Government moved in to bail it out. The reports are pretty damning. While I cannot go into all the details, I believe we should take note of a couple of points. First, the Hitchman Report found that the files in these banks were in a mess, so even in terms of the basic keeping of information, they were in trouble. Second, senior officiers and directors endorsed questionable loans and the executives really did not understand the seriousness of the difficulty they were in as a financial institution. So the facts are beginning to come out and the picture is pretty dismal and disastrous.
These facts are crucially important right now because when the Government originally moved to try to prop up these banks, it did not have the facts. That is a tragedy. The Government espouses a commitment to the market-place. It claims to be a good economic manager, to know something about the economy and to be rescuing the Canadian economy from its present troubles and bringing about prosperity. But when it comes to dealing with two relatively small institutions in that sector of the economy, it has demonstrated complete and utter incompetence. The Canadian people are becoming aware that the Government is economically incompetent.
The Government rushed in to prop up these banks without having full understanding of their financial situation. That is why several months later it had to pull the plug. When the Government first stepped in, it was as if it stepped into a dark room without turning on the lights. It walked in where wiser men feared to tread. It rushed ahead without knowing what it was doing and it did this in order to try to preserve its public image of good economic managers. It tried to preserve the picture of a Government which was taking this country into prosperity. In fact, the Government shot itself in the foot.
The facts are coming out now about just what a terrible mess these banks were in, which shows that the Government acted in a situation without knowing what it was doing.
October 10, 1985

There are a few key points I want to make, Mr. Speaker. We are talking here about $875 million of the public's money to bail out uninsured depositors in these two banks. Everyone here could think of many useful ways of using $875 million other than as a worthless gesture in trying to rescue a couple of banks which were bankrupt in the first place. Let us contrast the way this Government is treating banks and the way it treats ordinary workers. When the banks came knocking on the door saying they were in trouble and wanted access to the public Treasury, the doors were thrown wide open. The Government, without adequate information, acted in support of the banks. Contrast that with the lack of concern shown by the Government for the people who work in the banks. I am thinking specifically right now of the workers who have organized a union in the Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce and who are struggling desperately to get a first and fair contract. Do we see any action by this Government to help that union? Not at all. All we get is utter silence. However, when the executives of these banks ask for assistance, the treasure house is opened and the money is just shovelled out.
The people who work in the C1BC Visa Centre have organized a union and are seeking a fair contract. They would like to have the support of the Government in that endeavour. We pride ourselves in this country on fairness, justice and freedom of association, all of which underpin collective bargaining in this country. Yet these workers are faced with a management which is offering a contract with no wage increases to employees who earn on the average $12 an hour. The bank has put forward the proposition that it should be able to reduce hours of work whenever it suits the bank and at the same time insist that part-time workers receive no overtime or shift premium, partial benefits or pension. Do we hear anything from the Government about that? Does the Government say to the banks that if it is going to support them financially they should treat their workers fairly? No, all we get from the Government side is utter silence.
The bank, in its offer to these workers, wants compulsory overtime and the right to fire an employee who has taken a part-time job elsewhere. The bank wants a contract under which employees would not take cases involving discrimination to the Human Rights Commission. Do we hear any outrage from the Government over the fact that the bank dares to offer that kind of contract to ordinary Canadians? The bank wants contract language which would exempt it from the provisions of the Canada Labour Code governing technological change. It also wants to be exempt from just cause provisions of a collective agreement.
In summary, Mr. Speaker, I want to make the point that when the bank executives came to the Government, it reacted very quickly and gave its full support to the banks. However, when workers are struggling for a fair and just contract, the Government is silent. It is important for the Government to realize that it is demonstrating not only the unfairness of the
Depositors Compensation
way in which it treats the elite of this country relative to ordinary Canadians, but it has also demonstrated to ordinary Canadians its incompetence in economic affairs. If it had simply done a little homework it would have known what a terrible financial mess this bank was in. The facts of the bankruptcies of the Canadian Commercial Bank are coming to light now and Canadians can now judge the Government and the folly of its actions.
It is time for the Government to wake up, to withdraw this legislation, and to make good use of the $875 million of public money that it is throwing away in a useless gesture to bail out uninsured depositors. The Government should have been prudent in the first place and acted on the full facts. If it had done so it would not now find itself in the situation of having to pour taxpayers' dollars down the drain at a time when there is great need for public money to be spent on daycare and employment programs.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to speak in the debate on Bill C-79. Unfortunately, the ten minutes I have this morning are less than adequate to describe to the House the incompetence shown by the Conservative Government in this matter. I would like to recall the amendment moved by the Leader of the Opposition, the Hon. Member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Turner) in an attempt to inject some common sense in a debate into which we have been drawn by the Conservatives. My leader proposed that the House decline to give second reading to this Bill because its principle is to permit payments of large but unspecified amounts of public monies to unspecified persons or corporations. I think it must be the first time in the history of the Parliament of Canada that a Government is asking parliamentarians to vote on a blank cheque of this size. We are talking about $875 million, to be taken from public funds provided by all Canadian taxpayers to compensate a few wealthy corporations and individuals in our society that normally would not be entitled to compensation.
The Liberal Party is opposed to this Bill, and that is why we presented this amendment. The Bill should not be passed by this House because it substantially denigrates parliamentary accountability for expenditure of public funds. The previous speaker clearly indicated how these $875 million could better spent. However, I will not dwell on this aspect, except to add that this morning, after reading the papers and the testimony of that experienced banker, Mr. George Hitchman, we realized how seriously the Government had misled the Members of this House and the people of Canada throughout this debate.
The initial explanations that were given-

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
I would like to draw the attention of the Hon. Member for Papineau (Mr. Ouellet) and the House to the fact that there is at this moment a commis-

October 10, 1985

sion of inquiry that is supposed to determine certain questions and that has received a rather broad mandate. I realize this is a difficult matter to rule on for the Chair, and I would ask you to be patient, but there are a certain number of issues which cannot be appropriately raised or dealt with in this debate. I am therefore asking all the Members of this House to be careful or to choose their words wisely in the course of this debate.

I can understand the Chair's and the Government's unwillingness to deal with the Government's incompetence, which was clearly demonstrated in this morning's newspapers which reported Mr. George Hitchman's testimony. I should like to quote from a newspaper clipping which clearly states that the Government in this matter could have acted quite differently. What we know is that a scheme to save the Commercial Bank of Canada was proposed to the Minister of State (Finance) (Mrs. McDougall) and was turned down by the Government. So we are far from the truth when we are told that the failure of this bank in Western Canada has been caused by the energy crisis. As you certainly remember, Mr. Speaker, that is the excuse the Tory Government used at the beginning of this mess. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) have told us. If the Commercial Bank of Canada has failed, it is because of the energy policy of the previous Liberal administration.
But we know now that if that bank has failed, it was only because it was badly administered, because its directors authorized bad loans and because of utter mismanagement. When a scheme was proposed to bail out this bank, this Tory Government chose to turn it down. If the Commercial Bank of Canada failed, therefore, we can reasonably say that it was partly because this Government turned down at the time a scheme to bail it out.
The Northland Bank is a second bank which is also in trouble. During this debate, my colleague the Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides (Mr. Garneau) has put forward a plan to save this bank. I hope all Members on the Government side will consider this proposal, because this second bank in Western Canada could be saved if the bail-out plan put forward by the Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides were to be accepted. When we are told that banks are now going bankrupt, Mr. Speaker, my response is this: if those banks go bankrupt it is because this Conservative Government has been intent on applying a political solution rather than an economic solution to that financial crisis which we are now going through. This is perfectly plain.
I will quote from an editorial written by Mr. Frederic Wagniere and published in La Presse on September 11, 1985. This is what he wrote:
By arranging the bail-out of the Commercial Bank in March, the Government did wrong, it made a disastrous goof.
Ottawa misjudged the situation: the Government underestimated the amount of capital needed to save the Commercial Bank, and it overestimated the banks'
willingness to save a competitor. That error in judgment is serious, and it is important that in the future, the Government, the Bank of Canada and the Inspector General of Banks should show a better understanding of our banking system.
And he concludes with the following remarks:
The Mulroney Government wanted to save a fledgling financial institution in a part of the country which finds it very hard to get over the impact of the depression.
So he said.
They overreacted by referring to a crisis of confidence in the banking system that only existed in their own imagination.
They will now have to live with the uncertainty which they themselves created.
This, Mr. Speaker, is the situation. It is clear. That journalist described it in a few words. We could have saved those banks had the Government acted more sensibly and more efficiently.
The Minister of State (Finance) (Mrs. McDougall) who introduced the Bill is not even here now, so I will refrain from making the charge I intended against her. I simply submit I have found her incompetent, irresponsible, and throughout the days that followed that bank fiasco, she has shown indescribable arrogance and self-complacency.
Today as we are told that a third bank is having problems, I think it is essential that the Government should assume its responsibilities and tell all Canadians that our banking system is strong, that it can overcome trials, that in spite of a few mistakes, the Government will learn from the painful lesson it was taught this summer, and will see that the situation is corrected to prevent any other bankruptcy in our banking system.
What I find totally incredible is that the Government is asking us to reimburse $875 million or so to persons unknown, to unidentified individuals and corporations. You know, Mr. Speaker, that under the current legislation, a small depositor who invests in a bank can be protected up to $60,000. Before concluding my comments, I would like to say this. The small depositors do not need the Bill now being considered. But who needs it then? The people who invested a few million dollars in that bank venture and are now sheltered under the cloak of anonymity by the Progressive Conservative Government. In my opinion, this is unacceptable, unfair, unspeakable and I shall vote against the Bill.

Mr. Speaker, I want to participate in the debate on this amendment to the bank bail-out Bill of Barbara's. The amendment proposed is correct, just, and fair. It says we ought not to proceed with second reading of this Bill, and I agree with that. Can we not have faith anymore in Conservatives being truly Conservative? Have they distroyed the confidence of the Canadian electorate that Conservatives would really act like Conservatives? Why can't Conservatives be true to their ideology? I know that
October 10, 1985

Members over there have said they are red Tories and blue Tories, and some have even said they are "suppositories". But can they not maintain a basic Conservative principle, a principle which I heard all about during the last election and over the eight years I was here? They criticized the Liberals for it. They said the Government should stay out of business; it is free enterprise which is going to build Canada and we have to get the Government off the backs of business. The Government should not be involved in business. The business of business is business. So what do we have in Bill C-79? What are they proposing? What they are proposing is to insert themselves into the bankruptcy process.
We have a process whereby there is deposit insurance and depositors are insured up to $60,000. The Conservatives are proposing to go beyond that. They are saying to the business people, the large corporations of this country, you took a risk when you went after the high interest rates that the Canadian Commercial Bank and the Northland Bank offered, but it does not matter. We will insure that risk as well. It is all right to chase after the higher return. We will take the risk out of business.
In my riding two years ago when the major employer closed down for nine months, workers lost their homes. They lost their homes because they could not make the mortgage payments and no bank and no Government came to bail them out. Not one.
In this particular instance we have the spectacle of a Conservative Government wedded to the free market free enterprise concept and then running in to bail out its buddies from Bay Street and Wall Street.
And maybe Saint-Jacques.

And maybe Saint-Jacques, the Hon. Member says. I accept the argument that some Conservative Members over there use that some of these depositors are municipalities like Kanata, some are hospitals and some are western credit unions. But why don't we apply the old Conservative truism that we pay on the basis of need? Why don't we apply a bail-out on a means test basis? Let the Citibank, the Chase Manhattan, Barclay's Bank, The Bank of Tokyo or The Bank of Singapore demonstrate a need. If they can prove that they need the 121 odd million dollars which have now been guaranteed by the Government, we would consider paying them. Why not apply the same principle which they were advocating for old age pensioners and for family allowances? Why not apply that to the Government's corporate friends? I suggest that Members opposite do that and not come in here and ask holus-bolus for a bail-out.
As well, this Bill is premature, because we now have a judicial inquiry into the whole collapse and bail-out of the Canadian Commercial Bank and the Northland Bank. Mr. Justice Estey is now conducting a judicial inquiry, and there are some very serious questions which need to be cleared up. One is the role of the Inspector General of Banks. What is his role, what is his function? What regulatory powers does he have and how does he use them? What is the role of the Bank
Depositors Compensation
of Canada in this mess? After all, it was the Governor of the Bank of Canada, Bouey the fourteenth, who was phoning The Globe and Mail at the time of the original bail-out last March and saying, oh, well, the CCB is a viable bank. What is his role in all this? What is the role of the Government in this whole mess? After all, it is the same Government which has put forward a Green Paper to deregulate the banking industry and allow the creation of all sorts of Schedule C banks. She wants to open it up now, to deregulate it, as if we did not have enough problems. Back in May, I believe it was, the Minister who approached Mr. Hitchman and asked him to go on the Board of directors of the Canadian Commercial Bank. He said: "No, I do not know enough about this bank and its loan practices; I would not think of doing that". In fact, that should have been a signal for the Government to take a good, hard look at the operations of that particular bank.
As we go through this judicial inquiry, all sorts of very serious questions are being raised. We require answers to those questions. What was the role of the Inspector General of Banks? What was the role of the Governor of the Bank of Canada? What was the role of the Government? What was the role of the auditors who were supposed to audit the banks? As a matter of fact, the auditors are quoted in Mr. Hitchman's Report as saying that the Canadian Commercial Bank was not as conservative in its loan practices as they would have liked. What was the role of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson)? What was the role of the Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDougall)? These questions must be answered before Parliament can open up the Treasury doors and shovel out some 800-odd million dollars. That is just a down payment; the prospect is that this amount could run to $2 billion before it is all over. Parliament has a responsibility. When it spends taxpayers' money, it has to account for it. We, as Members of Parliament, are no wiser today about the smelly business in the Canadian Commercial Bank fiasco than we were about the tuna affair. The Government should not proceed with the Bill at this particular point. As I said, we need the answers to those questions. It would be wise to hoist the Bill until we have received the report of the judicial inquiry.
The matter becomes more curious as we go. For example, in this morning's edition of The Globe and Mail, we see the Minister of State for Finance or the Government running off to persuade banks to support the Mercantile Bank. It is like a house of cards. We now have the Government doing exactly what it did last spring. It is encouraging the banks and provincial Governments to support a shaky situation. The same situation is developing with the Mercantile Bank. According to The Globe and Mail this morning, "Ottawa persuaded banks to support Mercantile". Taxpayers need some answers. Parliament needs some answers. This Bill should not be proceeded with until we have received answers to the questions which we have raised in the House.
Hon. Warren Allmand (Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine
East): Mr. Speaker, I am rising in opposition to Bill C-79

October 10, 1985
Depositors Compensation
which, as Hon. Members know, is a Bill to reimburse depositors with over $60,000 in the Canadian Commercial Bank and the Northland Bank. I am doing so because, as other Hon. Members have said, we are being asked to reimburse people who have not been identified. We do not know who they are.
It is very strange. We are being asked to vote for a Bill which is requesting between $800 million and $1 billion. On the one hand, the Government says that it believes in parliamentary reform, that Members of Parliament should be more involved in the process, that there should be a stronger committee system and so on. On the other hand, it asks us, as representatives of the Canadian people, to vote on this large sum of money without telling us who will receive it. We do not know whether they are foreign entrepreneurs, American, European or Japanese. We do not know even if they are large Canadian entrepreneurs. Entrepreneurs enter the market-place knowing that they have to take risks and knowing that the CDIC only insures deposits up to $60,000. These people put their money in the Canadian Commercial Bank because they would receive a benefit; a higher rate of interest, in certain cases. They took those risks as entrepreneurs. They knew about the CDIC limit of $60,000. We presume that there are large corporations involved, but we do not really know for sure. We are being asked to bail out these people by a Government which says that we must rely more and more upon the free market system.
As my hon. colleague who spoke earlier said, there is a certain ambivalence in the Conservative Party. That Party came to power and said that we must return to the free market system, that we should let the free market system be the ruling principle in business and economic matters. However, when we are faced with the bankruptcy of the Canadian Commercial Bank-and very likely, although it is not clear, a large number of corporate entrepreneurs are involved-the rules of the game change and we are asked to bail it out. This sets a very serious precedent for other situations of a similar nature which might arise.
Perhaps there would be some justification for helping small credit unions that are depositors, small municipalities or small pension funds, but we do not know how many credit unions or small municipalities are involved. In fact, we do not know how many large corporations are involved. We are being asked to sign a blank cheque of nearly $1 billion without the necessary information being given to us. We are supposed to represent Canadians in the spending of taxpayers' money, and we are being asked to write a blank cheque for the Government.
Last March, when the Government came to us and asked us to vote for a Bill, it was a crisis situation. I was led to believe that it was putting before us something which had been solidly researched, that the Government had done its homework, and that its proposals in March to bail out the Canadian Commercial Bank would put that bank back on its feet and make it profitable for shareholders and depositors. We took the word of the Ministers involved and of the Government that they had done their homework and that we had to vote quickly in order to put that bank back on its feet. We voted for it, but we were
misled by the Ministers involved. They did not do the audit which was necessary. They did not accept the advice of people who knew quite a bit about the situation. The Ministers did not participate in many of the negotiations which led to the bail-out package. We have the impression that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and certain Members of the Government and of the Cabinet were willing to put forward the bail-out proposal at any cost, just to save face, in the hope-

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. I am very sorry to interrupt the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East (Mr. Allmand), who is a well experienced Member of the House. I remind the Hon. Member, as 1 did the Hon. Member for Papineau (Mr. Ouellet), that the Chair is in a very difficult position today in this debate. A royal commission of inquiry is proceeding on this very issue. The general principle remains the same, that there is liberty of debate in the House, but in this specific case there is also a royal commission which has as its mandate to investigate the whole matter. We are in a difficult position today. I remind all Hon. Members of the House not to refer to what the commission has, as its mandate, to investigate and not to prejudice the ultimate decision of this royal commission of inquiry.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I can only respectfully submit, Mr. Speaker, that your limiting debate in this way means that what the Government is doing is a farce and the freedom of speech of the House of Commons is being impaired.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: To make it clear, there are precedents on this very issue. To simplify what I am trying to say today, there is a royal commission of inquiry that has the mandate to look into this matter, to hear evidence and to submit a report. In view of this, it would not be appropriate for Members of the House, in the context of this mandate, to prejudge or, if I could use the expression, to jump the gun on the conclusions of the report. Since the commission has received this mandate, let us let it go on with its work. Therefore, 1 am asking Hon. Members to be careful. I do take into account the fact that in general it is a principle of this House that we do have liberty of speech.
On a point of order, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The Hon. Member for Saint-Denis, on the same point of order, I presume?

Yes, Mr. Speaker. I would like to submit, with respect, before the Chair draws any conclusions, that if this Bill is adopted, and it will be, despite the speeches of the Opposition and no matter how my Opposition colleagues vote, it will eventually have to be referred to a parliamentary committee. Does the Chair mean that a parliamentary committee responsible for considering a Bill referred to it by Parliament for consideration after second reading and that will
October 10, 1985

have to go to work right away, would have to be limited in scope because there is a royal commission of inquiry as well? I find that absolutely incredible ... and you are getting close to a sub judice, since you called my colleague to order twice. Therefore, with all due respect, I find it rather hard to believe that just because there is a royal commission of inquiry, practically everything becomes sub judice, and that while in Quorum, which we get daily, the first page tells us exactly what happened yesterday, Parliament should be deprived of its duty to consider a Bill that is before the House. The Government introduced the Bill, not the Opposition. The Government asked for a commission of inquiry, not a royal commission of inquiry, but it was the Government that asked for and set up this commission. So I submit, with respect, since I know you have a legal mind and I think we should discuss this, that it was the Government's decision to introduce a Bill. It also decided to submit the entire matter to a Justice of the Supreme Court, and now we are being told here in the House, although it was in all the papers this morning, that the Members of the House of Commons, who have a mandate to consider a Bill introduced by the Government, may not allude to what is happening somewhere else-
I do not know how the Chair intends to decide or rule on this matter, but with respect, Mr. Speaker, I think that my colleagues should be allowed to continue their present approach to this debate, without considering what is happening elsewhere.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
I shall, if I may, attempt a reply after listening with great interest to the Hon. Member for Saint-Denis (Mr. Prud'homme), who, as usual, has submitted arguments that reflect his experience in this House. Perhaps I may remind the House that I am somewhat reluctant to rise today and call Members to order on this question. I repeat that this is a very difficult situation for the Chair.
You are asking me a question indirectly, and since you mentioned my legal mind, I would like to inform the House that the Chair is not in the habit of making obiter dicta on questions that arise in the House, not on this matter or any other matter. Furthermore, we have the following situation: a commission of inquiry is considering a matter and will eventually have to submit recommendations. What we are asking the Members of this House today, and I suppose we cannot impose the same conditions on the media to which you referred, is that Hon. Certainly, there is a Bill before the House. That is clear. You have the right to discuss the matter, but you are being

Mr. Speaker, I am resuming the debate that was interrupted by the points of order and your own attempt to call me to order. I might say that I appreciate the fact that there is a judicial commission looking into this matter. However, this Bill is also before the House and we have to vote on it. There is a certain overlap in the subject matter covered by the Bill and the subject matter of the judicial inquiry. The points I am trying to make are important for the debate because the Government is asking us to support a Bill which is a second attempt to deal with the Canadian Commercial Bank situation. I have to put on the record the fact that I am opposing this Bill at this time because we were misled the last time. I do not intend to be taken in twice. I have to put the facts on the record with respect to that point.
Finally, I would like to make it clear that under our constitutional system the Parliament of Canada is the supreme court of this land. There is nothing else which is more sovereign or more supreme under our Constitution than Parliament. We are not subject or limited in any way to any judicial inquiry or any royal commission. I do not want to suggest in any way that the commission be pre-empted from doing any work that it should do. However, I intend to put on the record as fully as possible in the short time that I have all arguments which relate to this Bill.
I have said that I felt we were misled the last time and I gave some examples with respect to that point. I also wish to say that the reason we were willing to believe the Government the last time was that we were told it supports regional banks. It was under Liberal Governments that several of these regional banks were set up. We think all the arguments for regional banks are good ones. It is not right to have westerners running to Toronto and Montreal for approval of loans and so on. I think that is wrong. In this country there is certainly a place for regional banks and we are in support of that. We went for the first bail-out on the information given to us, but we found out it was wrong. Again, I ask: Why did the bail-out group not consult the Canadian Commercial Bank's external auditors? Why did the bail-out group not look at the minutes of the Canadian Commercial Bank audit committee? Why did the Government and the Minister turn down the banks' offer of a full audit of the bank's books? I could go on asking questions.
What is interesting about this whole question is that if there was one thing that the Canadian people expected from a Conservative Government it was good economic management. We did not expect this Government to be strong on social policy. We did not expect it to be strong on foreign affairs or other matters; but we thought it would be a good economic manager. However, before us we have a situation in which the Government was sloppy. The Ministers were sloppy. They were negligent. They did not perform the audits required, nor did they do their homework. They were cynical and smug about the whole issue. They did everything quickly and they
asked us to vote for something. They asked the Canadian people to support something without doing the work which is required of responsible Ministers when a great deal of taxpayers' money is involved. What is damning about this whole issue is that the Ministers did it quickly without the work that should have been done in the first place. They did it sloppily, negligently and carelessly and now they are being asked to bail them out again.
The other question to consider is: Where will all this end? We are talking about between $800 million and $1 billion. If we accept the precedent that we must bail out depositors who are depositing over $60,000, where will it end? Is this just more ad hockery? Is this another situation in which there is no consistent policy on the part of the Government?
I do not intend to give a blank cheque to the Government. 1 will not ask the Canadian people to support any Bill which would give a blank cheque to the Government. I want to reach outside Parliament because it seems that with the large majority which this Government has, and with only 70 Members in opposition, the only way we can change the Government's mind is to appeal over its head to the people of Canada as we did with respect to the Bill to deindex old age pensions. 1 beg Canadians to look closely at this matter. I ask: What does this do to our priorities? The Government is asking us to spend $800 million on this matter. How does that line up with other matters such as family benefits, certain environmental questions, assistance to our native people and a great many other important matters which have to be undertaken in the country? Is this really where we should put $800 million or $1 billion? I say no; but I ask Canadians and our journalists to focus attention on these issues so that we can bring pressure to bear on the large group of Government Members who seem not to be saying very much in opposition to this very important question, even in contradiction to their own principles of free enterprise and the free market system. They are willing to violate that principle in this case because it is politically expedient to do so.
We will vote in favour of the amendment put forward by the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner). We will not vote in favour of the Bill because we are not receiving the information we want. We do not know who will be the beneficiaries of this Bill. We feel it is contrary to all the principles of parliamentary responsibility to support a Bill such as the one before us.

Mr. Speaker, thank you for recognizing me as the next Member to speak in this debate. The amendment presented states that this House declines to give second reading, that is, approval in principle, to a Bill, the principle of which is to permit payments of large, but unspecified amounts of public moneys to unspecified persons or corporations, thereby substantially denigrating parliamentary accountability for expenditure of public funds. I think
October 10, 1985

it is a good amendment. I will vote in favour of it and 1 wish to tell Hon. Members why.
Before I do that, I would like to address some remarks covered by the press this week. I am referring to remarks made in Vancouver by Mr. Edward Kaiser who is the Chairman of the Bank of British Columbia. Mr. Kaiser registered his concern with respect to the whole issue before us, he being the chairman of a small western Canadian bank. He criticized parliamentarians for attacking the Government on this issue. As a Member of Parliament from Vancouver where that bank is based, I would like to spend a few moments addressing Mr. Kaiser's remarks. I wish to say to him and to the House through you, Mr. Speaker, that I agree with him and I disagree with him. I wish to tell the House why.
I agree with him in the sense that it is pretty clear that we need to have some stability and confidence re-established in the Canadian banking system, especially the regional banking system which, as the previous participant in the debate expressed in his speech, is very important for the economic viability of the country, especially for the western Canadian region. Like Mr. Kaiser I, too, am unhappy with the rumours about the liquidity of the Bank of British Columbia, the Mercantile Bank of Canada and the Continental Bank. I wish to say to Mr. Kaiser that we have not been saying that there are problems with those banks. As far as I know there are no problems being experienced by those banks, especially the Bank of British Columbia which, I understand, is in an excellent position. I used to have an account in Mr. Kaiser's bank. When I return next week to Vancouver I tell Mr. Kaiser that I will place a little bit of the little money I have-being a Scotsman I don't have that much and I am careful with where I put it-in his bank to show my good faith in the Bank of British Columbia. I think it is a strong and important bank. I want Mr. Kaiser to understand that we are saying that.
I also want Mr. Kaiser to understand that our job here in the House is to ensure that the Canadian banking system is working. When one looks at the fact that we are being asked to spend $1 billion to bail out another bank-and we bailed one out a few months ago-and when we look at some of the evidence upon which I will comment later, about the banking system and banking practices in Canada, then it seems to me it is worth doing this job. It is a job which the Opposition is undertaking, not with relish. We do not want people removing money from their bank accounts. We want a strong Canadian banking system. We want a strong economy in western Canada.
I wish to buttress what I have been saying with an article from The Globe and Mail. I will just read the first paragraph. It says:
The long-awaited Hitchman report on the Canadian Commercial Bank paints a damning portrait of a financial organization in which the files were a mess, senior officers and directors alike endorsed questionable loans and executives did not know how serious their problems were.
I will not go into the details of that. I only raise it to show that it is our job in the Opposition to ensure that these inadequacies with respect to the banking system will not

happen again. It is our job to put the Government on the hot seat in order that it will respond. The Government has a problem in a general way. It was giving very soothing assurances through Government regulators that these two western banks were in good shape. Contrast that, Mr. Speaker, with what is coming out in the Hitchman Report. The Government gave the word of the Governor of the Bank of Canada earlier on this year when it first bailed out the Canadian Commercial Bank. The argument the Government makes, I suppose, is that it agreed that these banks would be okay and, therefore, when the banks finally collapsed, it should morally and ethically bail out the depositors, not just for the $60,000 for which they were insured, but for the full amount of their deposits. That, of course, is unusual in the free market system where when people invest they take risks and if they lose, they lose, and if they gain, they gain. But the Government feels morally and ethically bound to bail out these banks, and that is one of the central parts of this debate today.
The second argument the Government would make, I suppose, is that it has to bail out these banks to the full extent of the deposits in order to ensure the stability of the banking system, which is the greater goal. I would think that these are the two main arguments of the Government and I would say they are false and dangerous arguments.
What do the people say in my riding? A 58 year old labourer who is unemployed asks, "Are you going to bail me out of my mortgage situation?" Someone else who is unemployed asks, "Are you going to bail me out? I don't have any money and I can't get another job". I know of a bank employee who was fired after 30 years of working for the bank because she had a nervous breakdown. Did the bank bail her out? Did it provide an early retirement and look after her? No, it just got rid of her. Ordinary Canadians look at these situations and ask, "Who is getting bailed out?" By and large, as far as we can figure out, after a lot of effort on the part of the Opposition and stonewalling on the part of the Government, we are bailing out foreign banks. We are giving a lot of money to foreign banks and to rich people. There may be a few poor people who could use their life savings and so on and perhaps we should establish a hardship fund for those people. But by and large these foreign banks do not need a hardship fund. The large Canadian banks are making lots of money presently and have in the last decade. We do not have to bail them out in this situation.
There is a feeling amongst the ordinary Canadians in my riding that there is a tremendous inequality here. Why should we bail out these people when we do not even know who they are? And we have evidence that we are basically bailing out foreign banks. The ordinary Canadians say that that is not fair. So I say to the Government, with respect to its argument, that it has to do this to keep the stability of the banking system that we must reform the banking system. We have to create a better regulated banking system. Some of the practices which were revealed by the Hitchman Report will be reported on in greater detail, such as speculative real estate loans, loans to

The Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDougall) said in the House that she inherited this terrible system. I am distressed when the Associate Minister of National Defence (Mr. Andre) stands up and blames it all on the National Energy Program and on us for supporting that program. We in the New Democratic Party did not support the National Energy Program. I have the votes here to prove it. That is a myth. I ask Hon. Members to take a look at the record and the votes. The National Energy Program hurt western Canada, that is true, but at the same time Alberta's problem is that it had a boom and bust situation. It is simple to blame the National Energy Program and to say that we are somehow anti-West because we feel we must look into the bail-out of these banks, but that is a red herring.
I would like to say in summation, Mr. Speaker, that we in the Opposition will not be fooled a second time. We are not going to agree to this bail-out. We were fooled with the first bail-out but we will not be fooled with this bail-out. If the Government asks the ordinary Canadians it will find out that they do not like bailing out foreign banks and real estate speculators. We are prepared to keep this debate going and to resist this legislation as much as we can. I tell Mr. Kaiser in summation that he should look at the Opposition's role in that respect. I will send him a copy of my speech and if I get a chance to speak again in this debate, I will read his reply into the record.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Turner) presented a motion which I will read slowly so that we can all understand exactly what it states, and I quote:
This House declines to give second reading to a Bill, the principle of which is to permit payments of large, but unspecified amounts of public moneys to unspecified persons or corporations, thereby substantially denigrating parliamentary accountability for expenditure of public funds.
I have not heard any Hon. Member speaking about what unites all of us here in this Chamber, and that is, the great tradition of the British parliamentary system. What we see at this time is a slow erosion of one of the best political systems, the Canadian parliamentary system which is based upon the British parliamentary system. The basic principle of the British parliamentary system is accountability. But the Government is asking us to vote blindly certain sums of money to unspecified persons or corporations. That is totally against the principles of this parliamentary system.
It is the duty of the Canadian Government to justify every expenditure of money. It is the duty of Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition and the other Opposition Party to oppose this Bill if we do not know what the money will be used for or who will receive it.
I will not, Mr. Speaker, talk about the event which took place yesterday in court. Mr. Hitchman was the first witness and others will come along and say something else so I do not want to prejudge anything, but he clearly said yesterday that the real subject matter was not what we were told in recent weeks. My colleague and friend-the name of his riding is so long I would rather say the Hon. Warren Allmand, but the rules say that I must say my colleague, the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East-said many of the things I wanted to say so I will not repeat them except to say that we were, in our evaluation, fooled once. There is a proverb, and my colleague from the NDP just said it, that we will not be fooled again. We all know the proverb that says, you can fool me once and shame on you, but if you fool me twice, shame on me. I can tell you that the Opposition will not, without fighting to the very last minute, be fooled twice.
You have heard recently, and my very good friend the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) himself said, that the Opposition is against the interest of the West. I think my friend from Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East very clearly said that we created these western banks and we were very pleased and proud, and no one is going to say that we are happy to see them in difficulty. We created them because we believe that everyone should have an equal share, not in the wealth of this country but in the decision-making power centre, and that is why it was so important to have these two banks and other financial institutions created in the West. It was in the interests, first, of the West, but of course also in those of the majority of Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, we do not think we should vote blindly, and for the benefit of my French-speaking colleagues and our viewers I want to repeat the motion of the Right Hon. Member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Turner), the Leader of the Liberal Party, the Leader of the Official Opposition. As he said to the House, we maintain that:
-this House declines to give second reading to a Bill, the principle of which is to permit payments of large, but unspecified amounts of public monies-
-and I emphasize this-
-to unspecified persons or corporations, thereby substantially denigrating Parliamentary accountability-
Mr. Speaker, how can I explain, how can the Ministers and Government Members, how can we Members of the Official Opposition and of the New Democratic Party explain to our constituents that we are about to vote blindly on a piece of legislation whose economic impact will be far-reaching? We are talking about at least $875 million to be paid to people whom we do not even know, foreign banks, American banks which are not even prepared to cooperate with Canada and tell us how such deposits could have been made with those branches and those banks. They want to keep us in the dark, but the Government is getting ready to pay them huge amounts of money.
October 10, 1985

Have we thought for a moment what we could do with that money? What can we tell other Canadians who call us to ask: Listen, I made a bad investment recently, the deal went sour. Now that precedents are about to be created, will the Government come to my rescue? How do we answer those people?
What can we tell them? I might say that the present legislation is sound, it was introduced by the previous Government. All those who have savings of less than $60,000 can sleep tight, they are fully insured. But the others who were prepared to take a chance and invest millions of dollars because the yield was better are having second thoughts now that things are going badly. They expect the Minister of State (Finance) (Mrs. McDougall) and the Prime Minister to come to their rescue, because everything goes these days, a real free for all. I see my colleague is smiling, but the fact is that we do not know what to expect next, anything can happen when the truth is hidden. Who are those people who pleaded with the Minister of Finance to have this Bill adopted? Who are those big wheels, those rich people? We can believe anything. Who pleaded with the Prime Minister who said to him: "Save us, we wanted to run a risk but things turned out badly, now please save us!" I remember that when the Opposition parties requested an emergency debate on the disasters befalling both those banks, the Government flatly refused. More than five Members opposite having risen and asked for a vote, the bells rang for a few moments and suddenly the Government changed its mind and asked us not to proceed with a vote because they would allow that emergency debate. We refused, we asked for a vote and the Minister of Finance as well as the Minister of State (Finance) after having said there was no emergency that afternoon, cringed and voted with the Opposition saying that there was cause indeed for an emergency debate.
We then saw the Minister of Finance leaving this House not to return; we saw the Minister of State (Finance) engaging in debate while she should have quieted the fears, because a Minister of Finance in Canada should not be as partisan as some of us may sometimes be. She was there to comfort us but that evening she delivered one of the worst partisan speeches that I have ever heard from a Minister of Finance during my 22 years as a member of Parliament.
1 would then say to you, Mr. Speaker, that the Opposition is not in the mood to vote blindly for that Bill. We will continue to demand, Mr. Speaker, by all possible means at our disposal under our Standing Orders, we will continue to demand- [English]
-demand, not request, but demand from this Government that we want to know to whom we are giving this money. People wish to know. The electors, the Canadian voters, are requesting us to fight in this House and not blindly vote sums of money to unknown people, unspecified corporations or persons. You can be assured, Mr. Speaker, that we are not going to rest and let this Bill go without fighting with every means at our disposal.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to make a few comments on Bill C-79 which provides for a bail-out of incompetence in these banks and in the Conservative Government. To be specific, we are dealing right now with an amendment which says that we do not give consent to second reading of this Bill. However, it is important to remember just what we are discussing here. We are discussing a bail-out which will cost some $875 million of taxpayers' money to pay depositors who had more than $60,000 on deposit at either the Canadian Commercial Bank or the Northland Bank. We must remember that depositors of up to $60,000 are fully covered by the Canadian Deposit Insurance Corporation and those who have more on deposit are covered for the first $60,000. Very few of the people in my riding will ever have more than $60,000 on deposit in any bank.
Upon looking at the very incomplete figures that have been provided through the profile of depositors in these two banks, we Find that this Bill is far from helping the little people of Canada. Seventy per cent of the funds will go to Canadian banks, foreign banks, investment dealers, large corporations, and provincial Governments. We must remember that this Bill does not deal with the needs of ordinary Canadians who, if they are lucky enough to have any money in the bank at all, very seldom have more than $60,000 on deposit. The $875 million which is called for in Bill C-79 amounts to asking every man, woman, and child in Canada to pay over $30. I apply that figure to my riding and ask what could be done with an additional $3 million in that area in terms of job creation and economic stimulus and in terms of helping community groups which are trying to develop alternate economic strategies in the face of the massive collapse of the economy which took place in British Columbia over the last two or three years.
Thirty dollars for every person on Vancouver Island would amount to $15 million. For the last year we have been thinking of the proposal of the Vancouver Island mayors that the federal Government should contribute to the $22.5 million forestry program that they have suggested. They feel that that program would provide jobs today and tomorrow, would ensure our forestry resource base, and would work toward a solid economy for that region. That program has been endorsed by the provincial Government, although that Government has not contributed any money to it. The Minister of State for Forestry (Mr. Merrithew) in the Conservative Government says that it is a good program, although he has only given the magnificent sum of $1 toward it. This money would really help the economy but, instead, the people of Vancouver Island are being asked to pay their share of this national bill for two incompetent banks. Instead of money coming on to Vancouver Island to help revive the economy, an extra $15 million is going off the island to bail out the incompetence of the banks and of the Government.
I respect your request, Mr. Speaker, that we be cautious and prudent in reference to the Estey Commission which is dealing with this subject. However, I want to emphasize that the

Government has put both yourself as Speaker, and us, as Members of Parliament, in a very difficult position by proceeding with a Bill with which we so strongly disagree at the same time as the subject matter is referred to the Estey Commission. Your request, Mr. Speaker, that we be very cautious and prudent in referring to some of these matters gives a point to the amendment that we are discussing, namely, that we not give agreement to second reading at the present time.
I have no desire to prejudice the results of the Estey commission, but I think that some of the initial evidence that has been heard by that commission is most relevant to our debate on Bill C-79. We on this side would be most remiss if we did not bring that to the attention of the Canadian public. Hon. Members opposite should pay particular attention to some of that evidence, and I would like to see some of them on their feet, either defending it or asking questions of the Government. I am sure that in the ridings of all Hon. Members opposite the preponderance of people are facing very difficult times. How do they square their consciences with going into their ridings and saying that they will be taking $30 from every man, woman, and child to bail out a couple of incompetent banks because the Government made a mistake last month? I would like to hear some Conservatives saying what they think about this Bill.
Yesterday there was evidence presented to the Estey inquiry by Mr. Hitchman, whose report was made available to the Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDougall) on August 12. That report gave a very clear picture of a bank that did not know what it was doing, and when it did know what it was doing it was doing things wrongly. I would like to read very briefly from a summary of things contained in this report on the bank. It says that:
-almost half of the Edmonton-based CCB's loans may have been worthless at the end of May, even after a March rescue organized by the federal Government had taken $255 million of bad loans off the CCB's books.
Of the $2.4 billion in loans on the CCB's books, the retired bankers said, either $910 million or $1.06 billion-depending on which calculation is used- should be written off.
But they quoted CCB President Gerald McLaughlan as telling them in July that the bank was planning to make provisions for loan losses of only $45 million this year. In its last annual report, a year ago, the CCB allowed for only $14.8 million in loan losses.
The Hitchman Report says that these problems did not arise in the last little while but, rather, some of these loans were problem loans the day they were made. The summary continues:
During the same seven-month period from October to May, non-earning loans-those on which the CCB was not collecting interest-rose from $147.8 million, 6.26 per cent of its loans outstanding, to a staggering $458.2 million, 19.31 per cent of the total. Of the 84 loan accounts reviewed by Mr. Hitchman and his colleagues, 28 had no financial statements attached, 11 had financial statements more than a year old and the other 45 included financial statements, but lacked enough detail to make a proper assessment of the loans. Only Canadian loans were studied, since there were no files in Canada for any of the CCB's loans in the United States.
The report pointed to some of the unacceptable practices. It said:
It was also unacceptable to collect past due interest and provide for future interest payments simply by increasing the amount of the loan and to collect a fee on such loans, subsequently including such fees in the bank's profits and raising the amount of the loan.
In other words, Mr. Speaker, this is a picture of both incompetence and some rather cute practices on the part of the bank. This report was in the hands of the Minister in August, but she took no action until the Labour Day weekend. Now we are being asked to approve this Bill, which will require $30 from every man, woman, and child in Canada. An $875 million bail-out for that kind of incompetence is not something that we can agree to.
I have received letters referring to this kind of bail-out as a betrayal of Conservative principles. It certainly is that. 1 contrast that with the treatment of people on Vancouver Island who invested in Victoria Mortgage Corporation which was incorporated under British Columbia law. When that failed, they had no deposit insurance because it was not registered with the Deposit Insurance Corporation. Yet, because the people who invested in Victoria Mortgage are relatively unsophisticated investors, they lose everything. The people we are talking about, who invested in CCB, had over $60,000 invested. They should have known better. However, we are rushing to provide a bail-out of $875 million for them. Nothing is being done for other people, like those with the Victoria Mortgage Corporation. The contrast is unacceptable. We find the Bill unacceptable.
