Mir. Jacques Guilbault (Saint-Jacques): Mr. Speaker, I also want to speak for a few minutes on Bill C-79. First, I wish to say that ten-minutes speeches on such an important subject seem too short in my view.
My leader, the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Turner), has moved the following amendment in the House:
This House declines to give second reading to a Bill, the principle of which is to permit payments of large, but unspecified amounts of public monies to unspecified persons or corporations, thereby substantially denigrating parliamentary accountability for expenditure of public funds.
First, Mr. Speaker, this amendment describes very clearly the position of the Liberal Party of Canada, which is to oppose this legislation, since a reasoned amendment such as this one objects to the very principle of a bill. We oppose this bill because what the Government is essentially asking us to do is to agree to a blank cheque of $875 million which would then be shared among a large number of depositors, even though we do not know their names or the amounts each one would receive.
Government Members are still hiding behind the confidentiality provisions of the Bank Act.
I must point out, Mr. Speaker, that the Official Opposition has at no time before, neither in the House of Commons nor elsewhere asked for publication of the names of the depositors
October 10, 1985

or the amounts of the deposits in any bank in Canada. We are making this request now because this is a quite abnormal situation. As the representatives of the people, we simply want to do our duty which is to know where this money is going, how it will be sent and why.
Mr. Speaker, we are faced with a liquidation situation. The Government has therefore decided to do with a bank what creditors do with a business which is having problems and can no longer repay its debts. A bank in liquidation is like a business which is going bankrupt, and in such a case, the creditor who wishes to recover part of the money he is owed must make an application and expect this name to be published. This is always the case. We therefore suggest that, in abnormal conditions such as a bank liquidation, the Government has no choice but to provide Parliament with the names of all depositors who wish to be reimbursed and the amounts they will claim.
Why are we faced with liquidation? Because the Government made a wrong decision and decided to overlook the recommendations of the Hitchman report the Government itself had asked a great expert in the Canadian banking situation to prepare. Mr. Hitchman had examined the various options open to the Government. Of course, there was liquidation, but there was another solution he found much more logical and which he recommended, but it was unfortunately not the one chosen by the Government. As concerns liquidation, Mr. Hitchman did not recommend it and pointed out two dangers of such an action. First, the cost would be very high, and these are his exact words:

"The cost is unknown now but will be a very large sum of money". The phrase "very large sum" is printed in block letters in his report. He also went on to say that if the Government chose the liquidation route, "We would be dependent on the ability and the resources of people in the liquidators' organizations who have no experience in liquidating assets of a bank in Canada".

This means that this Government, in spite of the warnings given by the expert who had been asked to report, has chosen to override his recommendations and done the opposite of what Mr. Hitchman had recommended. Because actually Mr. Hitchman recommended a two-point plan. First, the assets, other securities and loan portfolio should be assigned to the six chartered banks, and divided among them in order that they may manage them. The Government has chosen not to follow that recommendation.
Also, Mr. Hitchman suggested the setting up of a task force with genuine powers, the responsibility of which would be, first, to take over complete control of the operations of the Canadian Commercial Bank, to dispose of the remaining assets and to report every month to the Minister of State (Finance) (Mrs. McDougall). Also, he recommended that an
Depositors Compensation
investigation conducted concerning the operations of the Canadian Commercial Bank, with a report to the Minister of State (Finance). How is it, Mr. Speaker, that the Government, after hiring such a recognized expert as Mr. Hitchman, decided to override his recommendations, to come before Parliament and ask for a $875 million blank cheque, with the idea that we, Opposition Members, were going to forfeit all our responsibilities, which are to monitor public expenditures?
In fact, I am asking these questions, Mr. Speaker: What are this Government's priorities? Are they concerned with helping those who are most in need? This is not clear to me, from the measures the Government has put forward until now. Are its priorities, for instance, concerned with helping families in need? This does not seem to be the case, because they intend to deindex family allowances. They even intended to deindex old age security pensions. And they only backed down when there was a public out cry. Do they intend to prevent job losses that are occurring throughout Canada, and most tragically now in the East End of Montreal, where the industrial base is being eroded? No, Mr. Speaker, those do not seem to be the priorities of this Government which stated only two days ago, through the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mrs. Carney), that it was not ready to help Motoco buy the Gulf refinery, an operation which would save 450 jobs.
In fact, the Government's priorities seem to be to compensate large depositors, the ones with deposits exceeding $60,000, because all the smaller depositors are already reimbursed under the Deposit Insurance Act.
In fact, what I think the Government is trying to do is to conceal its previous errors. The Government, which arranged a poor bail-out program that has actually flopped, is now cornered. They were scared to do what they had to do, which was to follow Mr. Hitchman's advice. It would have required a lot more courage, a lot more competence from the Government, to ensure for months on end the day-to-day monitoring of a faltering bank, and thereby to protect all its depositors and by the same token the average taxpayer of Canada who would not have had to contribute such large amounts as this Government is now getting ready to pay out. The reason is the Government goofed beyond measure when it arranged that rescue package, and is afraid of following the appropriate recommendation, which is to keep the Canadian Commercial Bank in operation, to ask chartered banks to continue their support and extend their technical help to the Canadian Commercial Bank. It was this same Government that turned down an offer by the chartered banks to inspect the loan portfolio of the Canadian Commercial Bank. It was an ill-considered rescue package, and with the legislation now before us, history is repeating itself.
It is no surprise, Mr. Speaker, that on this side of the House, we are unwilling to accept the legislation put forward by this Government. It is an ill-conceived Bill. We are going to fight against it, and we are committed on behalf of the Canadian

October 10, 1985
Depositors Compensation
people to ask here and now a number of questions from the Government. Why did they not follow the recommendations presented to them? Why did the Government choose the winding-up route, which was considered as most dangerous by the expert, Mr. Hitchman? The Government will have to answer all those questions before they can expect the Official Opposition to give their support and allow them to sign a $875 million blank cheque. We will not accept that, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, it is somewhat unwillingly that I take part in this debate which, as my colleague the Hon. Member for Saint-Denis (Mr. Pru-d'homme) pointed out, is breaking with all Parliamentary traditions. How is it that we are called upon today to deal with Bill C-79, Mr. Speaker? I feel it is important to remind the House of the events which have culminated in this colossal fiasco.
Last March, Mr. Speaker, the Minister of State (Finance) (Mrs. McDougall), the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) gave the House every assurance that the Commercial Bank of Canada could and would be saved. Based on these assurances, Hon. Members on this side of the House decided to go along with the Government, because they felt it was necessary to save this institution and because they thought these three individuals had done their homework.
You can imagine just how surprised we were when we realized a few months later that, not satisfied with lying deliberately to the House, the Government had failed to do its homework and created a mess which will cost Canadian taxpayers an arm and a leg.
Mr. Speaker, we have learned, to our dismay, that the Minister of State (Finance) has put together a package to bail out the bank without even checking the bank's books. We have learned also that at the height of the crisis, the Minister of State (Finance) has failed to keep abreast of the new developments, preferring to go to Europe at a time when $1 billion in our taxpayers' money was in jeopardy. In my opinion, this was the epitomy of irresponsibility!
Absolutely!
Today, the House is being called upon to make up for the blunder of the Minister of State (Finance) by asking the Canadian people to spend $875 million.
That is outright incompetence!

Mr. Speaker, that is certainly the biggest bill Canadians have ever had or will ever have to foot to save the skin of an incompetent minister. If you listened to what they are saying throughout the land, you would realize that they are not at all happy with the part they have to play in this cover-up operation and the contribution they will have to make at the end of the line.
Mr. Speaker, we know that these decisions were made hastily-
The Government panicked.

We know the Prime Minister was too busy taking care of his image at the Economic Summit to spend time on this particular question which has now come before the House. Mr. Speaker, what is the Prime Minister asking us to do today? What is the Minister of State (Finance) asking us to do? They are asking us to save their skins, and to spend $875 million, not for the little guy but for depositors who had more than $60,000 in the bank, for depositors who knew that deposit insurance would cover the first $60,000 and who decided to take a risk in order to get a better rate of interest.
Mr. Speaker, today, this Government has the nerve to ask Canadian taxpayers to please save these money bags! Mr. Speaker, it is a little like telling the Minister of State (Finance) to go to Las Vegas and if she played for money and lost, not to worry-the Government would pay the bill. Mr. Speaker, that is exactly what the Minister of State (Finance) is asking us to do today. In fact, what she is asking is even more incredible, namely that we give her a blank cheque. Last March she told us: "Just trust me, I'll save the bank", and today she is telling us: "Trust me, I am going to make payments as I see Fit". We all find this rather alarming, Mr. Speaker. Why should taxpayers trust a Minister who deceived them once before, and tell her: Sure, we will give you a blank cheque for $875 million and you can give the money to whomever you want.
Mr. Speaker, this is . . . My hon. friend says that is the price you pay for incompetence. I must say it is a very high price. In fact, it is hard to imagine what $875 million represents. Well, you could build 15,000 homes and buy 100,000 cars with $875 million. Mr. Speaker, that amount of money would pay for all kinds of projects in ridings throughout Quebec.
I see the Hon. Member for Drummond (Mr. Guilbault) is in the House, and I am sure that he would prefer the money to be used to support projects in his riding. I am sure the Hon. Member for Argenteuil-Papineau (Mrs. Bourgault), whose riding needs funds for highway construction and that sort of thing cannot vote in favour of given away $875 million to anonymous recipients. Mr. Speaker, I know that you yourself have projects you are concerned about and that you will not approve this particular priority of this Government.
Mr. Speaker, I think we have here an example of glaring incompetence, and we must ask ourselves: What duties does me have as the administrator of public property and public funds? Does this Government have the right to use taxpayers' money to compensate a minority that is better off than the average taxpayer in this country? Is it morally correct to take money out of the pocket of the small taxpayer and give it to somebody else who already has more than $60,000 in a bank account? In my judgment, Mr. Speaker, that can only be done by someone whose conscience is asleep or who has something to hide. Never in this Parliament have we heard of a Government asking the House for a blank cheque. 1 doubt whether a
October 10, 1985

responsible Member would agree to give the Government a blank cheque. For instance, I know that the Hon. Member for Drummond would never sign such a blank cheque in his own business dealings. Knowing his business acumen and his sense of equity, I would expect him to oppose this measure.
We are creating an unbelievable precedent, for I am sure you too have read this morning's newspaper reports about other institutions being in trouble. We have all heard the interview given this morning by the Parliament Secretary to the Minister of State (Finance). He told the people of Quebec and the people of Canada that they should not depend on the banks. People used to say that the banks were as sturdy as a rock-
Who said that?

The Hon. Member for LaSalle (Mr. Lanth-ier). One has to wonder. He said that this morning. Can you imagine! Mr. Speaker, the Parliamentary Secretary himself has reservations about the credibility of our banking institutions. In his capacity he attends all Department briefings and has access to data unavailable to the House. Mr. Speaker, I am worried after hearing such a categorical statement from him. 1 hope, Mr. Speaker, that you have conveyed to your constituents the wise advice of the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Finance), to the Minister of Finance, because when an authorized spokesman for the Government questions the soundness of our banks, I am concerned. I have dutifully conveyed the message to my constituents following that interview.
1 think Bill C-79 cannot be allowed to go through subsequent stages. I do not think we can support that Bill and all Members of Parliament, even Government Members, should listen to their conscience and assume their responsibilities.
Mr. Speaker, accountability exists in public affairs. We are asked to give up that principle and I hope that during the discussions which will go on and on for months, because Canadians will never accept... and we hope that they will convince the Government that they are not ready to sacrifice themselves.

It must be recognized that the family is an important concept for Canadian men and women. The family is the basis of our society, our starting point in life and the focus of our growing environment. It is within the family that we learn about sharing, love and compassion.
Mr. Speaker, during National Family Week, we must also realize that the family faces all sorts of challenges in our society. Yet, it is a delicate entity in need of protection. The family is the most precious institution of our society. The family is a cell, and its members take care of their children and are proud of them. They are proud of their growth and their success. Mr. Speaker, we rarely recognize the value of the most important cell in our society, one which is at the very root of our personal and collective development.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as we all look forward to the Thanksgiving weekend, I am delighted that the residents of West Vancouver and the fishing community of British Columbia will have something special for which to be thankful. Today, on behalf of the Acting Minister of Fisheries and Oceans, I was delighted to announce that tenders will be called for the construction of a new fisheries research complex in West Vancouver. The Government's decision to proceed with this $8 million project shows its commitment to scientific research, to fisheries enhancement, and to economic development in the West.
Since the late 1960s dedicated research scientists have carried out a wide variety of fisheries research activities at the West Vancouver site, contributing significantly to salmon enhancement, aquaculture, habitat protection, and lake enrichment. They have worked in overcrowded, temporary facilities on the site of one of the first buildings on the North Shore, a fish cannery, which was built about 1891. Needless to say, the construction of these new facilities will provide much needed employment in the Lower Mainland area, reinforcing the Government's support of economic activity in British Columbia.
The work of the fisheries research scientists in West Vancouver has won international acclaim. Now, with new adequate facilities, they will be able to enhance further their contribution to maintaining healthy, vibrant commercial and sports fishing activities on the West Coast.

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mrs. McDougall that Bill C-79, an Act respecting the provision of compensation to depositors of Canada Commercial Bank, CCB Mortgage Investment Corporation and Northland Bank in respect to uninsured deposits, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee; and the amendment of Mr. Turner (Vancouver Quadra) (p. 7379).

Mr. Speaker, I am honoured to have the opportunity to speak on the battered bank bail-out Bill. This whole operation of bailing out the bank is almost incomprehensible to a layman. Many people across Canada take risks in their daily work. Every time a farmer plants a crop he takes a risk. He knows that there is a possibility that he will lose his investment. Every banker who makes a loan takes a risk. He knows that there is a possibility that that loan will not be repaid. The banks justify their interest charges by saying that they are taking a risk, may lose that money, and therefore must charge interest at a rate which will compensate them over the years. The banks recognize, just as well as the farmer does, that they may not be able to reclaim their investment on a particular loan. As the farmer does, they should prepare for the eventuality of not having that loan repaid.
The Canadian Commercial Bank obviously was not prepared to lose the money that was loaned and, over the years, was not prepared to back up those wrong decisions. This is not a matter of a farmer planting a crop and then being affected by the weather or by the conditions of that particular year. This is a bank which took a risk and by its bad judgment is now faced with the loss of those moneys loaned.
Why did they make those loans, Mr. Speaker? Obviously the purpose was to make more money. If we are to believe the reports which have been made, they made those loans knowing that they were providing that money at great risk. They made those loans without the kind of production we usually expect of an investment. For example, when a farmer spends money on his crop, he expects to produce something of value. When one purchases something at a store, one expects something of value in return. These banks made these loans and they expected

money in return without producing anything. I think that statement sums up the whole situation.
The western world has now reached the stage in the control and development of its economy where financing has become the most important part of any project. It does not make any sense. It is not a logical approach to the economy. The Government and its cohorts made much of trusting the market system. They suggested that by trusting the market system they could guarantee growth and prosperity. Obviously their confidence is often misplaced. In this particular case it was grossly misplaced. A dependence upon financing also involves a dependence upon the greed of people and organizations to work. The financial market system depends upon the greed of people. The greed of the Canadian Commercial Bank pushed it to make unsecured loans. In order to obtain money for those loans, the bank appealed to the greed of depositors by offering a point or two higher interest rate than was available on the general market. The actions of the bank and of the depositors were based upon greed, that is, they wanted to obtain more than they should have expected to obtain. This had a destabilizing effect and contributed to the downfall of the bank.
At one time a person went out to make a fortune or to earn a living by producing something. Apparently those days have gone. Now one makes a fortune by lending money and depending upon the greed of other people. We have reached a stage in our economy today when money is more important than production. We have been manipulated by the financial institutions to the point where production has become more dependent upon money than upon work. In any enterprise today, be it farming, small business or construction, it is seldom that the entrepreneur will make more profit than the bank or financial institution which lent the money in the first place. This seems to be backward. When the money-lender is the only person who is guaranteed profit in an enterprise, we are depending far too much upon money.
Even now as we in the House look into the downfall of the Northland Bank and the Canadian Commercial Bank, we should be looking at the basic financial structure of Canada. The values of the country have been changed to the point where production has less value than money and where it is possible to make money without any production. That was wrong when I was growing up, and it is wrong today.
Thus far almost $1 billion is being touted as the total amount necessary to bail out the depositors in the two banks. The Government has suggested that it will give only $48 million or one-twentieth of the bail-out amount to western farmers who find themselves in a disastrous situation because of drought. Who are the winners and who are the losers in this bail-out Bill? The borrowers and depositors are the winners; the losers are the taxpayers and to some extent the shareholders. Obviously someone will get this money. I hope that in the judicial investigation or elsewhere we will find out where the bail-out money is to go. Perhaps we require a list of borrowers as well as a list of depositors, so that Canadians will know not
only who is being repaid but who obtained money in the first place.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in the debate on Bill C-79. In this morning's edition of The Globe and Mail there was a report about the Canadian Commercial Bank which was headlined "CCB report describes bank in chaos". A more appropriate definition of what has occurred would be: "CCB report describes a Government in chaos".
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and the Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDougall) have mismanaged the affairs of these two banks. As a direct result of that political mismanagement, we are here today debating this Bill. The Minister stated that the purpose of this particular piece of legislation was to assist or bail out individuals who are uninsured depositors in the Canadian Commercial Bank and the Northland Bank. This Bill is an attempt to bail out two incompetent Ministers. The record speaks for itself in respect of what transpired in terms of these two banks.
We have been told today that we have a responsibility as parliamentarians to bail out uninsured depositors. Canadians are asking, as we in the Opposition are asking: Who are these people to whom Canadian taxpayers will have to pay $875 million? It is incumbent upon the Government, the Minister of Finance and the Minister of State for Finance to tell us and the people of Canada specifically who these people are.
Hon. Members know that depositors with less than $60,000 are insured; they are protected. Those with deposits of up to $60,000 are protected by law. Through this particular piece of legislation, the Government is asking that we bail out others who have on deposit in excess of $60,000. Why should we do that? Why should Canadians have to bail out individuals who have in excess of $60,000 on deposit in those two banks? The Minister has said it is because we have a moral obligation to do so.
Indeed, the Government might have a moral obligation. The Minister told the people of Canada, including those depositors, that the banks were on a solid footing and that, as a result of the bail-out made earlier this year, the banks were solvent and would survive. She was wrong. The Government was wrong. The Minister of Finance, the Minister of State for Finance and indeed the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and others misled the House. I am not suggesting that they misled the House deliberately but indeed they misled the House by saying that the banks would be sound if we supported the bail-out package. They were wrong.
Government Members told us that based on the best information available at the time, the bail-out would help the banks and the banks would survive. What information was available to the Government? We asked the two Ministers involved and the Prime Minister what information they had to give the undertaking to the Opposition and to the depositors of these two banks that the banks would survive. The fact is that they

did not have full information. Were they negligent in not obtaining all the information that was necessary to make such a crucial decision affecting so many Canadians?
Where was the Minister of State for Finance? A few short days ago, the Minister of State for Finance admitted to the House that she was not in Canada during the month of July, a crucial month in the unfortunate history of these two banks and the Government's involvement in them. What could possibly be more important than being in Canada to monitor the situation? We have been told that she was vacationing somewhere in Europe and indeed she told us that she was in telephone contact with officials. That is not good enough. We expect a Minister of the Crown who is responsible and accountable for the banks of Canada to be here in Canada when an issue of such importance and magnitude arises. No, the Minister had other priorities. Her vacation was more important than the issue of the Canadian Commercial Bank and the Northland Bank.
Where is the Minister of Finance? I can appreciate that the rules of the House dictate that Hon. Members cannot comment on the absence of a particular Member from the House. I am not going to comment on the fact that the Minister has been absent from the House but I would like to comment on the fact that the Minister is not in Canada. He has gone to some meeting in Europe. Some would argue that it is an important meeting of the IMF, but I would suggest to Hon. The Minister should be here in the House of Commons to answer questions put by opposition Members. He should be here to be held accountable for what is happening.

I began my discussion today by suggesting that we are seeing a Government in chaos. Indeed it is a Government in chaos. Canadians are asking who controls the finances of our country. The banking industry has been shaken by the collapse of these two banks and we are now told that a third bank may be in trouble. I would suggest that it is as a result of the incompetence of the Minister of Finance and the Minister of State for Finance that the banking industry is in trouble. Had they taken appropriate action in the early stages, the collapse of these two banks might have been avoided and Canadians would not be asked to pay out $875 million to uninsured depositors. We in Her Majesty's Loyal and Official Opposition are not prepared to give the Government a blank cheque.
The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) has moved an amendment which reads as follows:
This House declines to give second reading to a Bill, the principle of which is to permit payments of large, but unspecified amounts of public moneys to unspecified persons or corporations, thereby substantially denigrating parliamentary accountability for expenditure of public funds.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I wish to indicate on behalf of my constituents of York South-Weston that Canadians condemn the Government for its mismanagement of this particular matter. We hold the Government accountable for the failure of these two banks.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to address Bill C-79, an appalling measure that is before us today. The Canadian taxpayers are being asked to spend $875 million to bail out the uninsured depositors of the Canadian Commercial Bank and the Northland Bank. Canadians are quite scandalized that they should be asked to pay out this kind of money when the names of the individuals and corporations affected are not to be revealed. This runs entirely contrary to principles of accountability and it is entirely unacceptable.
We are very concerned about the financial priorities the Government is displaying in this bail-out Bill. We are concerned that the Government can find nearly $1 billion to make this pay-out, and indeed, by the time the pay-outs are finished, the sum may well be above $1 billion. We are concerned that the Government can suddenly find this amount of money when in its May Budget it proposed that old age pensions should be deindexed. We had to fight the Government on that measure, as we are currently fighting it with respect to the deindexation of the family allowance, a measure that would save approximately $200 million this year. The Government does not have that amount of money for child support programs because they are of low priority. Yet, it has nearly $1 billion, and possibly more, to pay out individuals, corporations, foreign banks, rich municipalities, large organizations and sophisticated investors who knew what they were doing. It can find money for these types of purposes which are surely less important than support of our social programs.
This is a matter which shows the Government at its most incompetent and its most negligent. The Minister of State for

Finance (Mrs. McDougall) has tried to blame previous Liberal Governments-and perhaps the blame should be shared-for the lack of improvement and the lack of attention to inspection procedures which would have made it possible to determine the failures of these two banks before a bail-out of this size would be needed. While I admit that perhaps some of the blame should be shared, I do not think that the explanation which the Minister of State for Finance has offered is remotely adequate enough. Certainly, all the blame cannot be placed where the Government wishes to place it. It is clear that the Government acted with insufficient information and that it did not obtain the information which it should have obtained.
Last March, it took the matter much too lightly when it announced its bail-out of the Canadian Commercial Bank. At that time depositors were told that the situation was solved and that with a certain modest sum of money the bank would survive. Indeed, right into the month of August the Minister of State for Finance was writing letters to inquirers stating that the long-term viability of the bank had been ensured and that it was in fine financial condition and that there was no need for concern. Simultaneouly, the major chartered banks were withdrawing their money, as were other investors, making it necessary for the Bank of Canada to infuse more money just to keep the bank going. It was one of the arrangements of the bail-out that the Bank of Canada would come to its rescue as there was a run on its deposits. Indeed, there was a run on its deposits and an enormous amount of taxpayers' money has gone into the continuing operations of these two banks under bad management and with large numbers of loans which were not viable. The whole mess was allowed to continue so that the bail-out with which we are now faced is considerably greater than it would have been if the Government had taken some responsibility and found the information it needed last March to come up with a more prudent decision at that time.
Let us consider the situation in which the Canadian Commercial Bank finds itself. It is a fairly young financial institution, having been incorporated in 1975 in Edmonton. Its loan portfolio was primarily western and very much in the risk sector. It was in the Field of construction, real estate and energy. Of course, one does not have to be very experienced in business, or in the economy, to know that these are sectors which are vulnerable to economic turn-around. Therefore, when there was a set-back in the energy field, that had an impact on the related fields of real estate and construction. When companies began to fold in the energy sector it meant the decline of the whole business sector. If construction is hit, people lose their jobs and move out of the province. As real estate markets are hit, people who once wanted to buy or build sell and leave for greener pastures. Here is a bank which very imprudently concentrated in a highly vulnerable area and did not learn its lessons in that area. It now wants the Canadian taxpayer to pay for its imprudent decisions.
Before us we have a further complication which, indeed, is a very sad one. The Canadian Commercial Bank bought into an American bank in California which was in a similar field with similar weaknesses. Initially, it bought a 40 per cent interest of
the Westland Bank. When that bank ran into financial difficulty the CCB bought the bank outright, supposedly to protect its investment. However, the Westland Bank had precisely the same type of over-concentration in vulnerable areas. Thus, we see the irony in western Canada when a set-back is experienced in the economy. They send their money out to purchase in an area which has precisely the same problems and is vulnerable to precisely the same economic downturns as the Alberta economy has been faced with. The failure of the California bank has certainly had an impact on the parent company in Alberta.
All of these difficulties did not just happen in July or August. They did not happen after the bank was bailed out in the first instance. This is information which was available. However, what we find is that the Government in setting the course which it did in March to bail out the Canadian Commercial Bank did so without obtaining full information. An estimate of bad loans or high risk loans was grossly under-estimated. It need not have been. It was simply that it did not require the information to be provided at the time. A hasty decision was made and, unfortunately, it was the wrong one.
I would like to read a statement made by the auditors of the Canadian Commercial Bank which they made in their appearance before the Finance Committee. It states:
A review of the annual reports and financial statements of the bank for the past three years clearly indicates a trend of declining net income, a rapidly escalating loss experience on loans coupled with very substantial increases in the total of non-earning loans and the percentage of non-earning loans to total loans.
In other words, information for a period of three years preceding the failure of the bank was like writing on the wall. What are non-earning loans? They are mistaken loans, loans that should not have been made. This information was in place but the Government did not insist that it be obtained and reviewed. It did not insist that an accurate estimate be made of the extent of the bad loans, the number of them or the bad decision making involved in them.
While we oppose the over-all bail-out, let me say that there is reason for the establishment of a hardship fund. There is reason to bail-out individuals and some groups which deposited their money, unsophisticated investors who certainly did not have any inside information and who would be particularly hurt. We think on a case-by-case basis these hardship interests should be considered. We are very much opposed to a blanket bail-out with no names attached. We oppose hard-earned taxpayer's money going to bail out foreign banks, large corporations and municipalities. This is an improper way for Parliament to be using taxpayers' money. We are profoundly opposed to this Bill.

Mr. Speaker, in participating in the debate on Bill C-79 one cannot refrain from commenting with respect to the conclusion which is emerging throughout the country in the minds of many Canadians who follow the activities and accidents of this Government. The Bill before us should actually be called the "Incompetence Bill" of the Government of Canada in 1985. As such, it would receive
October 10, 1985

five stars in any competition to determine the inability of a Bill to deal with the public's interest. We are debating today an amendment put forward by our Leader in which we urge this House to decline to give second reading to this Bill because the principle of the Bill is to permit payments of large but unspecified amounts of public monies to unspecified persons or corporations, thereby substantially denigrating parliamentary accountability for expenditure of public funds. I submit to you, Mr. Speaker, that this amendment is a perfectly legitimate amendment. It is consistent and falls squarely within the prerogative and traditions of Parliament. To be asked to permit payments of substantial sums blindly, so to speak, without the knowledge of who are the recipients, is a measure which would offend any parliamentarian worth his or her salt and would be deeply resented no matter what Party is in opposition. I am certain that the Conservative Party, if it was in opposition, would oppose this Bill tooth and nail, just as we are doing today. I wonder, therefore, how on earth this situation developed, considering the assurances which were given to us only six months ago in this House by the Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDougall). On March 25 she is reported in Hansard as stating:
We are satisfied that this Bank is now a viable Bank, that it will be profitable in the future, that we will be repaid as will other members of the support group out of the future profits of the Bank.
This was an undertaking. It was a clear statement. It was not conditional and there was no hedging about it. On the same occasion, on March 25, the Minister of State for Finance went on to say, and I quote:
This particular problem was triggered by something that happened within the bank's loan portfolio in California which then of course created problems with the organization as a whole.
The Minister did not, on that occasion, thank God, bring in the red herring of the National Energy Program as did some of her colleagues. She just identified the source of the problem. That was the position of the Minister at that time. The problem was not the bad economy in western Canada, nor was it the National Energy Program, it was the bank itself. The bank had invested very heavily, not in Canada but in Texas and California, into loans directed at the oil and gas industry. I am happy the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Miss Carney) is in the House today to hear this because I believe this Bill has relevance to her efforts in Canada as well.
She is here just for you.

I am very touched by that fact. The bank's investments were also directed to real estate in Texas and California. Six months ago we were given one set of assurances and six months later we must face a Bill which demands a phenomenal sum of money from the taxpayers of Canada without knowing who will be the recipients of the funds. The fact is that in March the Government made a political decision without searching and digging for the necessary facts. It made a decision based on partial information and it decided to do so because it felt that that was the political thing to do at the
Depositors Compensation
time. The Government cannot deny the fact that if it had made the effort to dig for the information, it would have been able to use it. However, the information was not used and by deciding not to use that information, it could not look at the facts. It disregarded a valuable tool which would probably have prompted this Government to make quite a different decision.
I was very impressed, Mr. Speaker, with the alternative course of action put forward in the course of this debate by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides (Mr. Gar-neau). He put forward a four-pronged approach by way of an alternative Bill. He recommended, among other things, that an investment be made in the equity of the Northland Bank and that, in his opinion, this should amount to $ 150 million to $200 million, and that the composition of the Board of Directors be changed to a more competent team. He also recommended that the Government of Canada guarantee the deposits in the Northland Bank for the next five years so that the depositors could regain confidence in this financial institution. I thought this was a rather constructive effort on the part of the Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides as he attempted to come to grips with this situation. He also put on record the fact that it is extremely difficult for us in this House of Commons to debate Bill C-79-the Progressive Conservative incompetence Bill-while at the same time the Estey Commission is trying to get to the facts which this Parliament does not as yet have. This exercise becomes even more difficult because it is, first, clouded by political incompetence and, second, it is carried out without full knowledge of all the facts. The Estey Commission exercise is taking place at the same time outside of this building in another place in an attempt to provide information to the public, and to the politicians, in order for them to do a proper job. For all of these reasons, Mr. Speaker, we have moved this amendment. It is highly reasonable that in order to approve the expenditure of $875 million, every Member of Parliament should know how these funds are to be expended. That is the basic thrust of our amendment and I commend it to you, Mr. Speaker, for your consideration, and that of the Government.

Mr. Speaker, I am glad for the chance to speak against Bill C-79. It is called the Financial Institution Depositors Compensation Act but everyone knows it simply as the tax bail-out Bill. This Bill is both unfair and destructive. People can accept something which is unfair if it is really needed and good for the country. People can accept something which perhaps costs the country a little bit but which creates a situation which is more fair. However, this is both unfair and destructive to the country.
We are being asked to approve an expenditure of $875 million now, and there is every reason to think that this is only the start. The Government will tell us how much more later on. What is notably unfair about it is that this money goes mostly to the very big depositors. These depositors looked around for a high interest rate and found it in this bank which was making questionable loans in order to get a high return. It

October 10, 1985
Depositors Compensation
turns out that for many months before last March there were suspicions in the banking community that the Canadian Commercial Bank was not operating in a prudent way. Yet the big banks, which should have and probably did know better because that is their business, took the risk and put their money in figuring: heads I win, tails you lose. If the CCB does all right, they get the profit. If not, they ask the Government and the taxpayers to pay their loss. That is where we are now.
Let us look at some of the CCB depositors. There was more than $108 million on deposit from foreign banks. There was $65 million on deposit from Canadian Schedule A and Schedule B banks. There was $1 million on deposit from trust companies. There was $56 million from investment dealers and brokers, and $51 million from other corporations. These outfits can stand to lose money better than the average worker or small business person. They can stand to lose it, not easily but better than most Canadians can, and they are also the ones who knew best what a risk they were running. By their own standards, they ought to pay for that risk because they demanded the profit that comes with the risk. When we ask these institutions why they take 6 per cent more interest on the money they lend out than they have to pay on the money they borrow, they say that is because of the risk. Now they have the profit for the risk but they want the taxpayers to bear the risk. That is what is unfair.
It is also very unfortunate, Mr. Speaker, that some other groups have put a good deal of money into this bank. I do not think they should have. The credit unions deposited $67 million. Municipal Governments deposited $30 million. Provincial Governments deposited $69 million. That is either taxpayers' money or the deposits of small business people and workers. That money should not have been put at risk. We used to have a principle that when money like that was in effect placed in someone's care, such as a municipal or provincial Government, credit union or union pension fund, it should be invested carefully. They should not take risk with what is essentially other people's money, particularly that of ordinary working people who cannot afford to lose it and who do not have any means of participating in the decision-making involved. However, that was a small part of the portfolio. In fact, between 40 per cent and 50 per cent of the total deposits were from Canadian and foreign banks. This situation is principally a rip-off by the banks who are happy to devour the carcass of one of their brothers and get the taxpayers to pay as much as possible of the risk that they take.
It is unfortunate in another way as well. There is a very interesting situation which illustrates the unfairness. The Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce has forced hundreds of its employees at its Visa Centre to go out on strike. It refuses to bargain in good faith and follow the 20th century concept of honest labour relations with its employees when they organize a union. This is one of the banks which is going to get money from the taxpayers, including those employees it has forced out on strike. They are being forced to subsidize an employer who refuses to let them have normal union rights. It may be only two or three hundred people but it symbolizes the policy
of not only the CIBC but of banks in general. They are very hostile to working people and small business people in this country. In fact, it is the working people and small business people who are being asked to shell out a total of $1 billion and it will soon be more than that, primarily to help the rich. That is what is unfair.
What is it that is destructive? There are many ways this money could be better spent. What does giving $108 million to foreign banks do for the Canadian working people who will have to pay it in the form of taxes? The banks do not pay much in taxes. Some years they do not pay any taxes at all, they get a rebate. If they make less than $200 million or $300 million they cry poor and get a tax rebate. Why should the taxpayer be foreced to pay $108 million to foreign banks? Indeed, why should working people be forced be forced to pay more than $100 million to Canadian banks over and above the donations already made over the years through a tax system rigged in favour of the banks? What if, for example, this money was spent on building homes? We need them. The Government says it has to cut back, and it did cut $29 million in the Budget for this purpose. Here is $1 billion which would easily build 20,000 homes and that would be a great deal better. It would employ unemployed construction workers and house people who the Government knows lack decent housing. We also know that the drinking water of Lake Ontario is dangerously polluted. The Government of the United States and, to some extent, the Government of Canada have allowed industry to dump their poisonous wastes into the Niagara River or on the land beside the river where it soon runs into the river. That is what we are getting in Lake Ontario. That is what they are drinking tonight throughout Metropolitan Toronto and many, many other communities around the lake. There are ways of reducing those poisons. There is new technology for purifying water but it costs money. The Government could do this but it says we do not have the money, and that is false. The Government does have the money. It has the money to go a long way toward purifying the water in Lake Ontario for millions and millions of people. Yet it refuses to spend the money in that way because it would rather give it to its friends in the banking system.
This is an unfair Bill, Mr. Speaker. It is destructive, it promotes unemployment in Canada, and prevents us from doing the things we need to do. It can provide housing and clean up the drinking water through which we can be poisoned by cancer-causing chemicals which industry has put in the water. I fully support the amendment of our Liberal colleagues and I hope this Bill will never see third reading.
October 10, 1985

subtopic: SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTIONS TO BE DEBATED

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTIONS TO BE DEBATED
speechtext: Pursuant to Standing Order 46, it is my duty to inform the House that the questions to be raised tonight at the time of adjournment are as follows: The Hon. Member for Halifax West (Mr. Crosby)-National Defence-(a) Compensation for sinking of the Lady Marjorie; the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow)-Consumer Affairs-(a) Discounting of income tax refunds. (b) Request that practice be banned.

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mrs. McDougall that Bill C-79, an Act respecting the provision of compensation to depositors of Canadian Commercial Bank, CCB Mortgage Investment Corporation and Northland Bank in respect of uninsured deposits, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee; and the amendment of Mr. Turner (Vancouver Quadra) (p. 7379).

Mr. Speaker, I, too, am very pleased on behalf of my Party to rise and address Bill C-79. As Members have stated before, it is basically a Bill to bail out the two banks which we have been debating for a number of months in this Chamber, namely, the Canadian Commercial Bank and the Northland Bank. Specifically stated, this Government is asking this Parliament, and this Party specifically, of course, to grant it a blank cheque to the tune of $875 million to pay for uninsured depositors of over $60,000. It would seem to me and, as I have learned from discussing this issue with constituents on the weekend, it would seem to constituents in York West, that the logical thing to do with respect to this Bill would be, at the very least, to tell this Parliament, and through this Parliament Canadians from one coast to another, who is going to be receiving this money. Yet, the Government comes to this Chamber and will not tell us where the money is going, just that we should co-sign the cheque and that we will be told later. Of course, Mr. Speaker, the individuals involved will have to make an application for reimbursement and their names will then become public. The Government is asking Parliament to put the cart before the horse.
Depositors Compensation
The Government goes on to say that if the Opposition Parties do not co-sign this $875 million cheque we will be against individuals, perhaps farmers, or some municipalities which must legitimately be reimbursed by Parliament. This Party is not prepared to say that we should not help the harder hit individuals on a case-by-case basis. However, if we were prepared to support that type of philosophy it would seem logical and appropriate that Parliament would be able to take a look at those individuals to determine whether we should be studying them on a case-by-case basis. However, the Government is not prepared to give us the names and the sources.
The Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDougall) rises in her place and says that we have a moral obligation to sign this cheque. What a perverse sense of definition, Mr. Speaker! The Minister of State bases her claim on morality. We on this side of the House ask where the morality was on March 25 when that Minister got up in her place and assured Parliament and the Canadian population at large that the Government knew what it was doing, that it had the appropriate information to lend the bail-out package which the House agreed to on March 25. I ask you today, based on the information that we have and on the inquiry information that is leaking out day after day, where the morality was on March 25 when that Minister assured the House that those banks would be viable if we approved the package. Now, Mr. Speaker, if we do not co-sign this blank cheque we are somehow going to be immoral about the entire affair.
Where was the morality of the Government when it knew about the mismanagement of the banks and continued to ask for support through Parliament? What about the bad administration and the 25 per cent of loans which were determined to be very risky and very poor in judgment and the poor documentation of the banks? Where was the morality of the Government, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), and the Minister of State for Finance when they did not tell this House and Canadians about the mismanagement? Where was the morality in not allowing this House to set up its own parliamentary committee to investigate those two banks and any other banking matters? Where was the morality of not allowing Parliamentarians to delve into the facts, to take a look at the depositors, to look at how much money individuals or farmers or municipalities had on deposit with those particular banks?
Where was the morality, Mr. Speaker, in hiding the political fortunes of the Minister of State for Finance, the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) himself by running to a Supreme Court Justice to have him take a look at the entire affair? Mr. Speaker, I do not say that to begrudge the integrity of any Supreme Court Justice, but because the individuals across the country have voted for the 282 men and women here Parliament has a moral obligation and a right to look into these questions without having to have a request through an outside body, let alone a judicial body, to look into what is purely and basically a politically motivated decision coming from the top of the Government.

October 10, 1985
Depositors Compensation
I ask you, Mr. Speaker, where is the morality in denying this Parliament a committee and where is the morality in refusing to get up during Question Period and answer questions genuinely asked, and in simply refusing to answer by saying that there is an inquiry? What are we doing here, Mr. Speaker? Why do these Ministers and the Prime Minister continue to come to Question Period if that is the type of answer that they are going to provide Canadians through this Chamber? Why bother at all, Mr. Speaker?
Where was the morality of the Budget that was introduced? They say that if we do not sign this blank cheque it will be immoral, yet the Government supposedly did not have the money, until Canadians made it change the policy to allow indexation for our senior citizens. In May it was saying that senior citizens had to help bring down the deficit and it was trying to legitimately justify something that could not be justified. It was the seniors of this country who forced the Government to reverse its perverse sense of logic absolutely lacking in morality.
Where is the morality in the deindexation of family allowances? It tried it with seniors and did not succeed so now the Government is hitting the mothers and children of the country. The Government says it has to remove indexation because it does not have the money in the coffer, yet it has the morality to turn around and ask for billions of dollars to bail out these banks. Where was the morality in the Budget which provided that as a result of all taxes, hidden and unhidden, by 1990 a family earning $15,000 to $20,000 is going to face a 36 per cent increase while a person earning $200,000 is going to face a 2 per cent increase? Where is the morality in that, Mr. Speaker? Yet the Minister of State comes to us today and tells us to sign the $875 million cheque. Is she serious? Is the Government serious? Canadians are laughing at the Government. It is unfortunate that Canadians are laughing at a serious and very delicate issue, but they are laughing at the incompetence of the Government.
Where was the morality in eliminating the RHOSP programs that allowed young Canadian families to buy homes? They removed the RHOSP because Canada could not afford it, but now Canada can afford billions of dollars for these banks. There are small businessmen which cannot get the assistance of the federal Government to compete internationally with Germany, Great Britain and Japan because we do not have the money to subsidize contract negotiations. Two specific companies lost contracts because they did not have the financial backing of the Government.
I detest profoundly, as do my constituents, when the Government and the Minister of State for Finance say that if we do not sign the $875 million cheque we are immoral. I submit to you with all due respect, Mr. Speaker, that the actions and decisions leading to the fiasco of these banks is a reflection of the immorality that sits on the other side of the House. It is for that good reason that I am supporting the amendment put forward this morning by my Leader.

Mr. Speaker, I was quite intrigued by the argument presented by the Hon. Member for York West (Mr. Marchi) who questions the morality of the Government in this bail-out. While I suppose an argument can be made for a lack of morality, I do not know whether one could deem it immorality. Perhaps amorality is a much more likely and appropriate term since it is evident that the Government engages in rather too little thought to deliberately do something immoral. It is a Government of ineptitude. It is a Government that, on the evidence, does not give careful consideration to what it does.
We know that Hallowe'en is approaching and as it approaches we begin to think in terms of masquerades. Certainly from all that we have seen over the last few weeks, we see a group of people who are masquerading as a Government. They are pretending and seem to trip from one error to another, one pratfall to another with their masks hiding their true stupidity.
The other day we engaged in a brief discussion in this Chamber in examining what is transpiring within the context of what purports to be the Conservative philosophy. I believe it is worth repeating a couple of points raised at that time. As a result of its election, this Government has certainly dramatically encouraged the free enterprisers-especially those on the extreme right wing-to visit upon us all the slogans of the Darwinian notion of free market enterprise. These include the notion that we should get Government out of the board rooms of Canada, unleash free enterprise and get the Government off the backs of business people. It is a notion that there should be virtually no intervention on the part of the Government and that we should encourage risk taking because it is a tremendous stimulus to creativity and inventiveness. The very notion that one might lose is the process which encourages innovative approaches to economic development and growth.
Now we see a Government that is prepared to spend the money that belongs to ordinary Canadians, many of whom are suffering immeasurably in the present economic context, to pay for the losses of those who must have assumed by virtue of the return that they sought that there was a risk.
As my colleague, the Member for Spadina (Mr. Heap), has indicated, the differential between the cost of borrowing and the interest paid to depositors reflects that kind of risk. However, that risk has completely disappeared. Suddenly the Government is no longr interested in risk or a free enterprise economy without Government intervention. Now, the Government must rush in where I suggest others might have feared to tread. The Government's action has clearly denied its philosophy or shown us clearly that the philosophy was not as it was described at all. The Government is not opposed to welfare, it is just that the target is different.
It would have been at least tolerable to see this inconsistency in all of this debate, but as we have heard consistently in the debate, the Government says that all of this mess-it can be described as nothing else but an incompetently derived mess- is caused by an awful conspiracy on the part of the East to do
October 10, 1985

in the West and that the National Energy Program was part of that conspiration action.
The Government would have us believe that one need not examine the issues here. One only has to make sure that enough money is poured into these two banks to demonstrate that the Government is not against the West.
The fact is that the Hitchman Report and any other number of facts would have demonstrated the utter fallaciousness, if not the malevolence of that argument. That argument is the moral equivalent of racism. It is divisive, inappropriate and diverts us from looking at the real issues.
The real issues stem from the fact that a number of factors may have made it difficult to survive in the recessionary period during which the downfall of the banks was initiated. However, to suggest that the Liberals are responsible for the failure of the Northland Bank, as has been implied by the arguments inferred from the Government side, is so bizarre as to suggest that indeed perhaps there are elements of immorality in this situation. Mr. Hitchman has pointed out that any close examination of the practices of the Canadian Commercial Bank would have exposed sloppiness and ineptitude, if not crookedness. None of this was revealed.
When I think about the machinations surrounding this bank bail-out, I am reminded of a peom about the blind man and the elephant. Let me read the first verse of the poem, which is familiar to many people:
It was six men of Indostan To learning much inclined.
Who went to see the elephant (Though all of them were blind),
That each by observation Might satisfy his mind.
Of course, one blind man touched the elephant and thought it might be a tree, another thought it was a a snake and so on. This is analogous to the Inspector General of Banks looking at the CCB, the auditors looking at the CCB and Governor Bouey looking at the CCB, as well as the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) looking at the CCB. The result with which we are all familiar reminds us of the last verse of the poem which states:
So, oft in theologic wars The disputants, I ween,
Rail on in utter ignorance Of what each other mean.
And prate about an elephant Not one of them has seen!
Indeed, no one saw the bank. They poured money into the bank without ever seeing it. Mr. Hitchman has pointed out what should have been seen in the bank.
People in this country are suffering from inhumane tax measures directed at children. Let me cite one more quotation. It is very interesting in the present context. It states, "The Government can find hundreds of millions of dollars for bail-outs but the same Government refuses to allow our badly underfunded education system the money it needs to produce the highly trained manpower this country needs. Those are
Depositors Compensation
strange priorities, bizarre in the extreme". A Conservative said that, referring to a bail-out which is ant sized as compared to the elephant in this instance.
What is disturbing about this situation is that the Government talked about eliminating the deficit but now we see the spectacle of $1 billion being taken away from the taxpayers, which could have met the needs of ordinary Canadians, to bail out the Government and those involved in the bank as a result of their stupidity. This amendment must be passed.

Mr. Speaker, although not a financial expert, I thought it was my duty to take part in this debate where it concerns the motion by my leader to amend the motion on Bill C-79. I think the Bill should have been split in two, the purpose of the first part being to reimburse according to law, deposits not exceeding $60,000, and the second part would have been called Part II, for gamblers, because as far as amounts over and above $60,000 are concerned, only gamblers or people taking risks deposited their money with the Canadian Commercial Bank.
1 simply want to say there is a matter of principle at stake here. We have said that the prestige of our banks has not been affected. However, as far as the public is concerned, a crack has appeared in the solid structure of our banks. We all know that money is a sensitive matter. When people say that a bank is in bad shape, the first thing you know, depositors are withdrawing their savings.
If we consider this for a while, we realize that our Canadian banking institutions have always been strong and sound, with a formidable reputation and one of the best banking systems in the world. I am sure that our bankers, who have always worked quietly and unassumingly, will be able to repair this crack in the prestige of our Canadian banking system.
I may add that the Government has a duty to provide for regular inspection of our banks. In fact, that is why we have a system with inspectors who see to it that banking operations are carried out in a normal way that is beneficial to the public. In this particular case we are talking about new banks, and I want to refer more specifically to the Canadian Commercial Bank which was established in 1975. I think the Government had a duty to provide more and closer supervision than it did in the case of other institutions with an established reputation and the stability that is typical of our Canadian banking system. If we refer to Hansard when the bank was created in 1975, we find the following description of the bank's activities, in the Senate Debates:
They will specialize-
-the branches of this Bank-
-their lending in higher yielding business loans, resource financing, real estate financing, term loans, loans to small businesses, and the like.

October 10, 1985
Depositors Compensation
And also the following:
The risk that is sometimes associated with these assets will be minimized by close, specialized management and forms of insurance, such as mortgage insurance.
Mr. Speaker, with hindsight, it would appear that management was poor. That is why I am saying that perhaps this particular bank, like the Northland Bank, should have been the object of closer monitoring since it was a new bank. Ten years in the life of a bank is not very long, Mr. Speaker, but now we know what can happen: with assets of $40 million it ended up in a $4 billion-plus bankruptcy. Again I refer to the history of the creation of the bank in 1975. After the sponsors made their statements to convince the Senate that the Bill ought to be adopted, Senator Heath asked a very relevant question, and I quote:
Is there any provision for a restriction on the percentage of shares that can be owned or controlled by individual, corporate or government shareholders?
Here is Senator Hays' answer:
This will be a private bank, and its innovators would like to see, as principal shareholders, Canadian institutions, primarily pension plans. There may be 25 such institutions, each holding 4 per cent of the shares. There are laws to ensure percentage of holdings.
So no provision was made for shares held by individuals. Senator Molson found it rather strange-he still had a sharp mind with respect to financial matters-that the sponsor of the Bill would react like that, so he asked:
When my honourable friend says it will be a "wholesale" bank, does he mean there will be no phase of its activities that deals with the ordinary, small individual; that there will be no banking for the ordinary, small operator or depositor? I am not quite clear about the term "wholesale" in this case.
So there is the crux of the problem, Mr. Speaker, and that is what led to the collapse of the bank. It is unfortunate that at that time some senators managed, so to speak, to dig the grave of the bank even before it was born. For this reason, the various Governments should have paid a special attention to this bank from the start, since the basic principles were, should I say, perverted. According to a basic economic rule, the higher the yield, the higher the risk. All those institutions, organizations or Governments which had invested in this bank more then $60,000 wanted to make more money. It was high-risk capital, therefore, which should be excluded from this Bill, at least until we are advised of the names of those who will benefit from the Government's generosity.
The City of Hull, which is part of my own riding, had invested $12 million in this banking institution. Do you know why? Simply because it wanted to get more interest on its investment. In other words, it took a risk, and the people are going to suffer, but in the end they are likely to punish those they had elected not to risk the capital entrusted to them but to protect it. The duty of any appointed or elected administration of a public organization, municipality or group is to make sure that the invesments he or she makes on behalf of the community are secure investments and not high-risk ones. That is precisely the point I am trying to make and that is why
I will support this amendment, together with my colleagues, so that we do not waste the taxpayers' money to compensate those gamblers who invested more than the $60,000 limit of insured deposits.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have an opportunity to speak on Bill C-79 which is a proposal by the Government to bail-out a major bank in the country.
Before this debate began, before this issue was raised in the House of Commons, I, like most other Canadians, never gave too much thought to the banking industry. This debate has been a particular eye-opener for me and for average Canadians who are not involved in the field of high finances in their daily lives.
For example, I always considered the Inspector General of Banks to be just that. I always had the vision of some person who was high in authority and was in fact a general, in the sense that his main role would be to police the operations of the banking industry. It has come to light during this debate that the Inspector General of Banks has a total staff of some eight people to police the expenditures and investments of billions of dollars of ordinary Canadians' money. If we examine what the Inspector General and his staff of eight people are required to do, we find that they are financed and paid for by the banks. In other words, the banks are paying the Inspector General and his eight inspectors to police themselves. This may be one of the reasons that we find ourselves in the kind of difficulty with which we are faced today.
It must be realized that we are talking about a first instalment only. The House is being asked to provide a first instalment of $875 million of taxpayers' money. This money is not for people who invested or saved $ 1,000 in a bank account or even $5,000 or $6,000. All those people will be covered under depositors' insurance for investments up to $60,000. We are talking about $875 million of taxpayers' money, and 70 per cent of that amount will be directed to large corporations and foreign banks. We are talking about people who are used to high risk investments in the banking and financial industry. They knew what the risks were before putting money in. Having known that risk, they are now not prepared to absorb it. It looks as if the Government, in this Bill, fully supports what these corporations and foreign banks are demanding of Canadian taxpayers. It is totally unfair. What makes it doubly unfair is that the Government will not even tell us who are these people, making the argument that the information is confidential and that confidentiality would be harmed if Canadian taxpayers were told to whom they were paying this money. The Government argues legalities. Legalities or no legalities, Canadian taxpayers are entitled to that information.
As a Member of Parliament, I represent a constituency that does not have an over-abundance of rich people. My constituents work extremely hard for their money. They are fully entitled to that information so that they can make a judgment on whether or not the payment of $875 million is actually
October 10,1985

justified. What they have told me is that they do not see the justification for it and certainly do not accept the argument of the Government that depositors have to be protected both in name and in their investments. In fact, people have written to me on other issues and have made comparisons. When the Government decided to reduce the deficit, it made the argument that senior citizens were prepared to support its effort to do so by accepting the deindexation of their Old Age Security. The Government made the argument that senior citizens would accept that for the sake of the national economy. If I recall correctly, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) tagged on to that argument that as soon as the economy improved, the Government would try to move to improve pensions. I find it passing strange that the Government could put up that kind of argument in defence of attacking senior citizens, but could not put up the same one when it came to protecting foreign banks and large corporations. It had absolutely no difficulty reaching into the taxpayers' purse overnight to find $875 million as a first instalment, and the Government will come along later with a request for another several hundred million dollars for foreign banks and large corporations. The Government attempted to attack senior citizens until they said that enough was enough and made it back off. In addition, it proposed a reduction in transfer payments to the provinces for the provision of medicare and post-secondary education to the tune of $2 billion over the next five years or six years. What is the Government's argument for doing that? It is because the deficit is too large. It has to reduce the deficit, and it believes that the only way to do it is by going after people who are sick and who need assistance and by going after students who need assistance to attend university. That is how the Government wants to reduce the deficit, but it does not make the same argument when it comes to banks and corporations.
What about family allowances?

We know what the Government is trying to do to the family allowances. It is attacking families, women and children who are a major resource to the future of Canada. It has no compunctions in that regard, but it feels sorry for the corporations and for the foreign banks and goes out of its way to protect them.
There is a housing crisis in Canada. There are people in Metropolitan Toronto and elsewhere who cannot find decent, affordable housing. What is the Government doing about that? It is cutting back in the funding for housing under CMHC programs. If the Government was elected by Canadians to represent their best interest, it sure has a funny way of carrying out that mandate. If there is a shortage of affordable, adequate, good housing, surely the Government should be finding the money to stimulate housing growth in the public sector. It would not only provide a socially useful purpose; it would provide jobs. The more jobs created, the better the economy. It is general knowledge that for every job created in housing construction, another three to four jobs are created in spin-off industries, such as electrical manufacturing, appliance manufacturing, plumbing and housing materials. We could
Depositors Compensation
create many jobs in Canada if there was a political will to do it. The money is there. There is $875 million for the corporations and foreign banks, but there ain't any money for ordinary Canadians who need financial support at the present time.
In my remaining minute, let me indicate that I was a member of the Standing Committee on the Disabled and the Handicapped which produced a report containing 130 recommendations. To my knowledge the Government has hardly acted on any of them. The total amount of money required to implement every one of those recommendations would be less than 1 per cent of the total expenditure in the social services budget. If the Government seriously wanted to do something in the best interest of Canadians, and if it had the political will to do so, then that is the direction it would take. Mr. Speaker, it is with pleasure that I lend my support today to an amendment moved by the Right Hon. Leader of the Official Opposition, Mr. John Turner, the Member of Parliament for Vancouver Quadra.
Mr. Speaker, if I may, I would like to read this amendment:
This House declines to give second reading to a Bill, the principle of which is to permit payments of large, but unspecified amounts of public moneys to unspecified persons or corporations, thereby substantially denigrating parliamentary accountability for expenditure of public funds.
What are the important words in this amendment, Mr. Speaker? These words are, and I quote:
-large, but unspecified amounts-
I repeat, large, but unspecified amounts. Mr. Speaker, we are being asked to give blindly $875 million, and probably even more eventually.
In my humble opinion, it is shocking that, because of the lack of concern, the negligence and the incompetence of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), Member for Etobicoke Centre, and the Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDou-gall), Member for St. Paul's, the Government wants to bleed ordinary people, workers and small wage-earners.
Mr. Speaker, the amendment also says the following:
-to unspecified persons or corporations-
I would like to know which Conservative Member, which Government Member, in his own private business, would give a blank cheque to a company before seeing what he will be getting in return. Mr. Speaker, I think that this shows total incompetence. It is unacceptable. The Ministers have the audacity to ask us for an enormous blank cheque. As I have said, Mr. Speaker, I would very much like to see a Member on the other side make out a blank cheque to any business
