whatsoever without knowing what he will get for it. Canadians have the right to know where these $875 million are going.
How can we explain to the Canadian people what is going on? Who asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) for this Bill? What does the Bill introduced by the Minister of State for Finance hide? Mr. Speaker, has the Government examined what this will mean for the economy of our country? What will be the consequences of all this? The Ministers ask us to trust them. But what are we trusting them to do? We are signing what? We are paying out to whom? Who are the people, who are the corporations to whom we will be giving the money? Mr. Speaker, let me tell you that on this side of the House, we no longer have any confidence in this Government. We no longer have any confidence in its bad managers. We no longer have any confidence in this Progressive Conservative Government that is replete with incompetence people on that side of the House. Moreover, they are keeping from us the names of the beneficiaries, of those who will be receiving those $875 million, of those who will be receiving all that money. I submit to you, Mr. Speaker, that since that money belongs to the Canadian people, to every Canadian man and woman, we all are entitled to know, you Tory gentlemen, where you are going to put those $875 million.
Imagine for a moment what we could do . . . Madam Minister, you could pay attention, this will be of much interest to you also. Anyway, you were just elected in this House. Imagine, Mr. Speaker, what we could do with that money. Let us for a moment turn our mind to our senior citizens, let us consider for a moment the family allowances. Let us remember our poor mothers you want to deprive of their money, and think of the de-indexing of family allowances. Think of our senior citizens. They wanted to clip their wings off recently, cutting down part of the indexation. Think of senior citizens, of artists living on very small salaries.
Think also, and 1 am sorry the Minister of State (Small Businesses) (Mr. Bissonnette) is not in this House, yes, think a little, Mr. Minister, about the small and medium-sized businesses you claim you want to help. Instead of paying out those $875 million to people, to businesses the names of which you refuse to disclose . .. Are you hiding something, you Tories? Are you afraid to tell us whom this money will be going to? To people in the Montreal East End, to Quebecers, to Canadians of both sexes? subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   NUCLEAR ARMAMENTS ADVISABILITY OF DECLARING CANADA A NUCLEAR ARMS FREE ZONE
PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   NUCLEAR ARMAMENTS ADVISABILITY OF DECLARING CANADA A NUCLEAR ARMS FREE ZONE
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the Government should consider the advisability of declaring Canada a nuclear arms free zone by prohibiting the deployment, testing, construction and transportation of nuclear weapons and associated equipment through and within Canada, the export of goods and materials for use in the construciton and deployment of nuclear arms and further, the Government should encourage cities, provinces and states throughout the world to undertake similar action.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the terrible potential of nuclear weapons entered into the public consciousness shortly after the first atomic bomb was dropped on the Japanese cities of Hiroshima and Nagasaki. Never before had human beings unleashed such a powerful and concentrated form of destruction. Since that time, when the nuclear arsenal was very small, nuclear fire power has grown so that now it is estimated that there are more than 50,000 weapons in existence globally with a total explosive power equal to 1.5 million times that of the bomb which devastated Hiroshima. Every year the nuclear arsenal grows in destructiveness and sophistication.
Even if we pass this resolution, we will not solve the problem overnight. Canada is not a superpower. Canada does not have the ability to unilaterally end the arms race. However, as a middle power, with a well respected reputation as a peace keeper, Canada does have a role to play in preventing nuclear war.
Nuclear war is what is at stake here. I am not being melodramatic when I say what we have to worry about is the survival of the earth. If nuclear weapons are ever used, it will mean the complete destruction of human society. Some theorists talk about a limited or winable nuclear war. In my view, Mr. Speaker, this is pure folly and I believe it is understood as that by most people. The solution is not to develop better weapons to ensure our side will win in any conflict but to ensure that the stockpile of nuclear armaments is never used.
The destructive capability of nuclear weapons is well known. The missiles all over the world are posed and ready. There is little question that any nuclear engagement would surely escalate so that major population centres across the world would suffer severe damage. It is estimated that in an all-out nuclear war, 1,150,000,000 people would die and 1.1 billion people would be injured. These numbers would be considerably increased as the effects of radiation took their toll.
Those injured would not have access to medical help because the bulk of our medical facilities and personal are in the areas targeted by nuclear missiles. As it was put in an article in the United Nations Chronicle, and I quote:
The whole infrastructure required for dealing with serious injuries-operating rooms, nurses, blood, antibiotics, drugs, water supplies, electricity, telephones, heating, transport services-would be in disarray.
Nuclear Arms Free Zone
It goes on to state that those not killed or injured by the blast would be the victims of radiation.
It was not until 1962 that researchers discovered the existence of the phenomenon called electromagnetic pulse. It is a surge of electromagnetic energy caused by a nuclear explosion which disables telephones, radio, television, computers, radar systems and power grids. According to Princeton University physicist Daniel L. Stein, writing in the Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists, and I quote:
Even if permanently damaged, computer memories would be erased, digital systems might process incorrect signals, trajectories of missiles in flight could be altered, and power outages might occur.
The electromagnetic pulse means that there would be even less chance of a partial nuclear war being possible because with the failure of electronic communications across the world, who could be able to order a stop to the attack or counter-attack?
This is an example of the unknowns which we must face in the nuclear age. The power we are dealing with in nuclear weapons is awesome and irreversible but it is also largely unknown.
Another example is the recently discovered and widely discussed concept of nuclear winter. Even a much smaller number of nuclear devices than could be expected, say, in an all-out nuclear conflict, would cause serious environmental damage, making the earth a very inhospitable place. Aside from the short-term effects of nuclear blast and thermal waves, survivors would face extreme cold, water shortages, lack of food and fuel, heavy burden of radiation and pollutants, diseases and severe physilogical stress, all in twilight and darkness.	'
Another study released in January of this year by the Royal Society of Canada, on the environmental impact of nuclear war, concluded that a nuclear exchange between the superpowers would probably destroy Canadian agriculture even if no Canadian targets were bombed. It is frightening to think that this was nearly 40 years ago, after the development of nuclear weapons technology and before this particular effect became widely known. That makes me wonder what other results so far unimagined are going to be discovered.
There is no doubt that this escalation of the arms race has heightened the fears of not only Canadians but of people around the world that the threat of a nuclear exchange is indeed a real threat. All of this at a time when we should be developing programs to assist people around the world to live a better life is unforgivable. Moneys and other resources we put toward the arms race are money and resources which we cannot dedicate to providing safe drinking water to everyone in the world, eliminating illiteracy, improving health and developing agricultural resources. The United Nations sponsored a three-year study of the linkage between disarmament and development by 27 experts from every area of the world. The group concluded in its 1981 report that the world has a choice. It can continue to pursue the arms race or it can move with

October 10, 1985
Nuclear Arms Free Zone
deliberate speed toward a more sustainable economic and political order, but it cannot do both. The arms race and economic development are in a competitive relationship. Even the Brandt Report emphasized that one-half of 1 per cent of one year's military expenditures would pay for all the farm equipment needed to increase food production and approach self-sufficiency in food deficient, low-income countries by 1990.
In the developed world, military expenditures are often defended because of the alleged jobs they create. Everyone should know that in fact military spending is one of the least effective ways of providing people with employment. One of the supposed advantages of Canadian involvement in the Strategic Defence Initiative is its job creation potential. Any serious look at this proposal would show that in this area, as in many others, the SDI proposal is a bad one. Studies have shown that, in comparison to other uses of the same money, military spending is one of the least effective ways to stimulate job creation. U.S. Labour Department figures show that 28,000 jobs are created for every $1 billion spent on military procurement. That same amount would create 32,000 jobs if spent for public transit, 57,000 jobs if spent for personal consumption, or 71,000 jobs if spent on education. For those workers presently working in arms production, the solution is the conversion of those facilities to non-military and socially useful production. Obviously this cannot be done overnight and not without considerable research, but it is something the Government will be forced to consider over time.
As I said earlier, the proposal to make Canada a nuclear arms free zone will not solve all the world's problems with regard to the nuclear threat. It is, however, an appropriate response for Canada as a middle power in the world with a considerable reputation as a peace-keeper. By bringing about the aims of this resolution we would enhance Canada's reputation and prestige on the world stage and set an example for other countries.
After considerable controversy, Mr. Speaker, the previous Government acquiesced to U.S. requests to test the Cruise missile. The Conservatives, while in Opposition and now in Government, supported this decision. We in the NDP have opposed this testing all along. Canada has a considerable arms industry. Some manufacturers are involved in nuclear weapons technology. Litton Industries, which is working on the guidance system for the cruise missile, springs to mind. Several U.S. weapons with the potential to be nuclear armed when deployed were and are being tested at the Canadian Maritime Experimental and Test Range at Nanoose Bay on Vancouver Island. Included among these weapons is an anti-submarine rocket. This rocket is fired from surface ships, weighs half a ton and consists of a rocket motor and either a MK 46 torpedo or a nuclear depth bomb of one kiloton. With a range of six miles, this weapon is the primary anti-submarine warfare weapon of U.S. frigates, destroyers and some cruisers. It has been the U.S. military's policy to neither confirm nor deny whether American vessels visiting Nanoose and other bases in Canada carry nuclear weapons. Our Government is content to
leave it at that. Along with many other Canadians, I say that is not good enough. The intent of this resolution would prevent visiting vessels from carrying nuclear arms.
For over a year the Nanoose Conversion Campaign has had a peace camp at Nanoose to arouse public awareness about the possibility of submarines carrying nuclear arms. My colleague, the Hon. Member for Cowichan-Malahat-The-Islands (Mr. Manly), has raised the issue of whether visiting U.S. submarines at Nanoose Bay and Esquimalt are armed with nuclear-tipped Tomahawk cruise missiles. He has presented petitions to the House from people opposed to these vessels which are possibly armed with nuclear weapons. The Tomahawk has a range of 1,350 miles and, according to William M. Arkin, Director of the Arms Race and Nuclear Weapons Research Project of the Institute for Policy Studies in Washington, D.C., it is the nuclear weapon most likely to be in on the start of both World War III and World War IV. To quote Arkin a little further, the Tomahawk can also, the Navy believes, contribute to fighting a controlled and limited nuclear war. This concept is absurd and Canada should let the Americans know we think so. One way would be to forbid nuclear-armed Tomahawks in Canadian waters. The Canada-U.S. agreement for the base at Nanoose expires in April, 1986. Needless to say, this agreement should not be renewed. There are other examples of Canadian nuclear involvement. Our Department of Energy, Mines and Resources gathers gravitational data in the Arctic which is used to improve the accuracy and the counter-force capability of U.S. ballistic missiles. The Government recently came forward with its decision on star wars. Because of widespread and strong opposition to the Canadian participation in SDI, the Government declined the U.S. Government's invitation to participate directly in SDI research. It left the door open, however, for the participation of, and even grants and subsidies to, Canadian companies.
There has been considerable debate on the star wars issue in Canada. The NDP has come out solidly against the proposal. The theory of deterrence in nuclear strategy holds that because the U.S. and the U.S.S.R. have the ability to destroy each other, the threatened use of this ability in a retaliatory strike prevents one superpower from attacking the other. Although it is possible to question and challenge deterrence from a number of perspectives, no one in political or military power has advocated abandoning deterrence. The concern has been of technological advance which could give one side a momentary advantage over the other. Star wars is just that sort of destabilizing technology. Foreign policy, defence and strategic thinking would move from seeing nuclear weapons as an unthinkable retaliatory force, to nuclear war as a useable, potentially successful tool of international and military policy. According to the former U.S. Ambassador to the UN, George Ball, the SDI announcement in March, 1983, was "one of the most irresponsible acts by any head of state in modern times".
There are a number of reasons why star wars would not work. It is dangerous because it is the abandonment of deterrence by the United States. Star Wars will be destabilizing,
October 10, 1985

dangerous, costly and will never be able to make the United States safe from a nuclear attack.
Discussion of the concept of a nuclear weapons free zone has a long history in some parts of the world. In Canada the legislature of the Province of Manitoba passed a resolution declaring that province a nuclear weapons free zone. Over 80 municipalities in Canada have declared themselves nuclear weapons free zones. Last year nearly half a million Canadians signed a peace petition calling for, among other things, a nuclear weapons free zone in Canada.
The final report of the United Nations Special Session on Disarmament in 1978 declared that "the establishment of nuclear weapons free zones on the basis of arrangements freely arrived at among states in the region concerned constitutes an important disarmament initiative. The process of establishing such zones should be encouraged with the ultimate objective of achieving a world free of nuclear weapons".
This is an area in which Canada can play a responsible role in reducing nuclear tension. There is already an international agreement signed in 1967 prohibiting nuclear weapons in Latin America. In the Nordic countries proposals for a nuclear weapons free zone has become one of the most debated foreign policy initiatives. In 1983 the Finnish President discussed the prospect with then Soviet Prime Minister Andropov who declared that the Soviet Union was willing to discuss the possibility of including the Baltic Sea in such a zone. The discussions are a long way from being settled on this issue, but that this debate is even taking place is a hopeful sign.
The possibility of a nuclear free zone in the Balkans has been discussed by Bulgaria, Greece, Romania, Yugoslavia and Turkey. Progress has been limited in these multilateral talks, but the concept is frequently discussed in bilateral talks among the Balkan countries. According to Nikos Andrikos, a special counselor to Greek Prime Minister Andreas Papandreou, one must be optimistic that the denuclearization of the Balkans will soon become a reality.
The South Pacific is another area that is proposed as a nuclear free zone. In August of 1984, the leaders of the 13 member states of the South Pacific Forum endorsed an Australian proposal to establish a nuclear free zone in the region. There are some substantial differences of opinions between these states, but despite these differences they have been able to give their initial agreement to proceed based on the Australian formula.
It is time for Canada to take the initiative in this area. Canada has viewed its options too narrowly and has not been willing to take an independent enough foreign policy position. I do not agree with those who say that taking a more independent course will lessen the stability of the world. Making Canada a nuclear weapons free zone will set an example for others in the world and will be a concrete step toward making the world a safe place.
I hope that Members on the Government side do not opt to talk this resolution out as is often the case, but will take a
Nuclear Arms Free Zone
realistic and humanistic view of this resolution and agree to have it referred to committee where witnesses can appear to give testimony and where we will be able to listen to the views of ordinary Canadians who are extremely concerned and becoming increasingly so about this particular issue.
Finally, if the Government were to adopt a more mature attitude toward matters such as this, we could provide an awful lot of good to people who are less advantaged than us throughout the world. We could use the moneys we are spending on armament build-ups to serve that purpose. I hope that the Government Members have listened to me. I know that my good friend the Member for Simcoe North (Mr. Lewis) has. I can see it in his eyes and I know that he will be persuading the Members on that side of the House to come around to my point of view.

speakeroldname: Mr. Gerry Weiner (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   NUCLEAR ARMAMENTS ADVISABILITY OF DECLARING CANADA A NUCLEAR ARMS FREE ZONE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I consider it an honour and privilege to be able to speak on this subject this afternoon. When we discuss humane and realistic approaches, the position which Canada has taken with regard to human rights in the world today is the position we took when we went to the Soviet Union with the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark), and is a continuation of the position that we have taken in South Africa with regard to apartheid. We have taken this position with dignity and force in Central America and I look forward to being involved with human rights wherever there are people who suffer. For me it is an honour to be able to speak on this particular subject.
Last March 18 the House had a full debate on Bill C-218, an Act to declare Canada a Nuclear Weapons Free Zone. Today we are asked to debate the question of declaring Canada a nuclear arms free zone which would prohibit the deployment, testing, construction and transportation of nuclear weapons and associate equipment through and within Canada and the export of goods and materials for use in the construction and deployment of nuclear arms. From my point of view, there is no difference in substance between a nuclear weapons free zone and a nuclear arms free zone. This being the case, although the Government position on this matter has not changed between March 18 and today, this is a good opportunity to repeat certain aspects of our policy on nuclear weapons free or nuclear arms free zones.
On June 30, 1984 Canada removed the last remaining nuclear-tipped Genie air-to-air missiles which were to be used in wartime in an air defence role by Canadian CF-101 Voodoo interceptors. The air defence role has now been taken over by CF-18 aircraft which can do the same job using conventional weapons systems only. There are no nuclear weapons stationed on Canadian soil which is not the case, however, for at least eight of 16 members of NATO. Overflight of American aircraft with nuclear weapons, or port visits by nuclear-powered war ships, some of which may bear nuclear weapons, were they to occur, would do so only with the express permission of the Canadian Government. The same consultations and permission would be required for the deployment of any other nuclear weapons within Canadian territory.

October 10, 1985
Nuclear Arms Free Zone
Thus, while in some respects Canada may be regarded as a de facto nuclear weapons free zone following the withdrawal of the last nuclear capable aircraft from service with the Canadian Armed Forces, we continue to participate fully in the defence alliance, NATO, which employs a nuclear deterrent. Accordingly, possible comparisons with the practices of other countries which are not members of NATO are not particularly valid.
Canada is a member of the North Atlantic Alliance and has now been for more than 36 years. We joined the Alliance because we believed in the concept of collective security-a united effort to deter aggression or to counter it should conflict occur. There were many advantages to such an Alliance. However, the most telling advantages were then, and continue to be, the united strength which accrued to the Alliance enabling it to resist undue external political and military pressure to reduce the cost of defence by dispersing the burden of armaments among the member states.
Similarly, NATO has enabled the West to speak with a unified voice on critical issues of international security and to pursue the progressive development of east-west relations in a coherent fashion. It is an invaluable forum for nations such as Canada to express their views and to exert a constructive and moderating influence on the policy directions taken by the western powers in their relations vis-a-vis the East Bloc.
However, while Canada enjoys the collective security and influence given by membership in NATO, Canada also recognizes the need to share the burden of this collective security. It should be noted here that no NATO country has declared itself unilaterally a nuclear weapons free zone. As a point of clarification, Iceland has not declared itself a nuclear weapons free zone as has been erroneously reported in some news media. The Icelandic Parliament, in its resolution of last May, simply reiterated its old policy that no nuclear weapons be situated in Iceland without the prior consent of Icelandic authorities. The Icelandic Parliament has also envisaged that its Foreign Affairs Committee explore possible participation and further discussions of a nuclear weapons free zone in northern Europe encompassing an area from Greenland to the Ural Mountains.
The proposal to make Canada a nuclear arms free zone might have the effect of prohibiting the testing of the cruise missile in Canada. The decision by the previous Government to allow the United States to test unarmed air launched cruise missiles in Canada was seen as consistent with that Government's support for NATO's two-track policy which led to the deployment of ground-launched cruise and Pershing II missiles in several NATO European countries. This Government decided to allow the United States to continue with its testing program because it believes that the cruise missile is an essential element in the global balance of deterrence and is part of the western response to the modernization by the Soviet Union of its offensive and defensive nuclear systems
during the 1970s. This Soviet modernization continues into the 1980s.
It must also be remembered that NATO has had to rely on nuclear weapons to overcome the potential threat present in the great preponderance of Warsaw Pact conventional forces. It would not be in NATO's interest to give up the option of the possible use of nuclear weapons as a deterrent should the Warsaw Pact forces ever contemplate an attack on the West. At the same time, however, it should be noted that NATO upholds the United Nations Charter which lays down that all members shall settle their international disputes by peaceful means and that there be no use of force-any force-against the territorial integrity or political independence of any state.
The proposal would also prohibit the construction of any components of nuclear weapons in Canada. Regarding Canadian co-operation in the production of U.S. cruise missiles, Litton Systems Canada Limited was awarded the subcontract by the U.S. Department of Defence through its parent company in the United States, Litton Industries, to produce a portion of the inertial guidance system for the cruise missile. Litton's participation in a small part of the cruise missile vehicle program should not be taken as a change in Canadian policies instituted at the end of the 1960s to divest our armed forces of a nuclear weapon capability. It is, however, consistent with joint defence efforts with our NATO allies who rely in part on the maintenance of a credible nuclear deterrent in the face of the growing military threat from hostile forces.
The proposal before us today also calls for the Government to encourage cities, provinces and states throughout the world also to become nuclear weapons free zones. While someone else will speak on the question of regional nuclear weapons free zones, I would like to comment on the question of Canadian cities and provinces declaring themselves nuclear weapon free zones. We recognize that there is an important symbolic value in the declaration of a nuclear weapons free zone as an expression of the desire of mankind to be free from the threat of nuclear war. However, any responsible Government must look at the real implications of what a nuclear weapons free zone means from the point of view of security.
The Hon. Member has reminded us that there are over 50,000 nuclear weapons stockpiled, 90 per cent of them in the United States and Soviet Union with the other 10 per cent dispersed throughout the United Kingdom, France and China. There may be other countries with that same capability.
I remind the hon. gentleman that some 40 years ago, before the advent of the first nuclear weapon, mankind found ways of destroying tens of millions of lives during the Second World War. In another war, some 70 years ago, many others died. There were no nuclear weapons.
There is no doubt that the world today is subjected to strains and tensions that are unique in modern history. Humanity is faced with the awful alternatives of seeking a process to reduce international tensions or creeping to the brink of nuclear devastation. Therefore, we must all be heartened with the upcoming meeting between President Reagan and Secretary-
October 10, 1985

General Gorbachev in Geneva. That is where the issue should be discussed and where we may see hope and inspiration. We all hope that ways can be found to reduce nuclear and conventional weapons. This can be achieved when speaking together as friends with confidence in each other. Hopefully we can begin to lay down those arms that have destroyed so many lives. What a useless waste of mankind.
It is a difficult subject to address but I can say that it is a subject which is very dear to me. 1 have had immediate members of my family lose their lives in battle. We do not want to see that repeated with our grandchildren. We are at a point in history where we will not survive nuclear confrontation, nor can we afford a conventional war that might lead to the ultimate countdown.
Nuclear weapons cannot be disinvented. They are a terrifying reality which political leadership must seek to constrain. Yet, a failure to incorporate a credible nuclear component within NATO's over-all strategy would be an invitation to nuclear blackmail with consequences too terrible to contemplate. In this sense, the real question before us is how we can best achieve policies which will reduce the recourse to nuclear weapons in Europe and elsewhere. Our Party has approached this through three fundamental principles. Canada's foreign policy should rest on a bipartisan search for consensus. The cornerstone of our security is NATO solidarity and only through strengthening the non-nuclear deterrent can we reduce the present reliance on nuclear weapons.
In April, 1969, Prime Minister Trudeau unilaterally cut our NATO commitment in half, saying that Canada had no foreign policy of any importance except that which flowed from NATO and this was a false perspective for any country. Under that Prime Minister, defence spending as a percentage of Gross National Product had been cut by 30 per cent. This policy of wilful neglect of our contribution to the collective security of our alliance has led to a situation in which Canada spends less per capita on defence than any other nation in the NATO alliance, with the exception of Luxembourg.
The Hon. Member who presented the resolution today comes from a Party that would also want to remove us from NATO. He would pull us back from an alliance to which we are a party. We very much support that alliance and believe it is a cornerstone for peace. He wants us to bring our people home and shake that foundation.
This pattern of neglect of the conventional deterrent has damaged our reputation for reliability among our allies. Such neglect of a conventional deterrent has also contributed to an over reliance on nuclear weapons. A determined effort must be made to reduce our present dependence on a possible use of nuclear weapons by substantially improving the conventional component of our defence. We believe that the overwhelming majority of Canadians are prepared to accept this approach. That is why they gave us that overwhelming mandate on that famous day in September, 1984. That is how our Government plans to act.
I am glad that my hon. friend raised the issue of aid because that is a subject that is very dear to all of us who work in
Nuclear Arms Free Zone
External Affairs. It is probably one of our proudest accomplishments. We contributed some $1.8 billion in the last Budget to an aid program which is always geared to improving the quality of life for people whom we intend to help. It is never tied to political considerations, but based strictly on technical grounds. Whether it is Central America or elsewhere, we want to do what we can to improve the social and economic conditions of the people whom we are trying to help. We believe that is the basis for removing confrontation. We know that it will encourage people to talk to each other. Currently, there are many countries in the world whose young people are trained to do only one thing-to fight. They know no other end or no other approach. We have attempted to go to those areas to build programs that will give them a usefulness. Through this means I believe they will come to understand that by improving their quality of live they can build a better world for all of their citizens.
I will be an important moment when President Reagan and Secretary-General Gorbachev talk. There are many issues on the table, including nuclear weapons, Strategic Defence Initiatives and many other issues. As long as there is conversation and consultation, we can look forward to another generation of peace and tranquility. The last 40 years has not been bad for most of us.

Mr. Speaker, in view of the fact that this motion is being debated for the second time and that it is triggering a number of intense and committed interventions on every side of the House, I wonder whether it would not be the better approach to allow it to go to committee for full debate which would give it an opportunity to be fully examined by all interested Parties. It has an outlook and breadth of scope that, in consideration of the present international climate, deserves the full intention of all interested parliamentarians. It is with that thought in mind that I would urge the Government not to talk it out and not to put up other speakers but allow it to go through.
Therefore I will refrain from making the intervention I intended to make so as to give a signal to the Government that we would like very much to see this motion go to committee.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   NUCLEAR ARMAMENTS ADVISABILITY OF DECLARING CANADA A NUCLEAR ARMS FREE ZONE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to speak on a subject that is very important to me: nuclear deterrence and a Canada without nuclear arms. The formidable power conferred by nuclear energy has probably created the greatest dilemma of this century. One of nature's powers which man is now only starting to learn to control, this power is neither good nor evil. Solar energy, another form of nuclear fusion, is essential to life on this planet. If it is misused in nuclear arms, atomic energy may well put an end to humanity as we know it today. Controlled nuclear energy can help man in his daily life. It can cure diseases or be a source of destruction. How we use it will determine whether this kind of energy is good or evil.

October 10, 1985
Nuclear Arms Free Zone
Nuclear arms exist already, and we cannot make them disappear that easily. We know that one of the goals of Canada's foreign policy is, and has been for a long time, the ultimate elimination of all nuclear arms. Books such as The Fate of the Earth by Johnathan Schell, films like If You Love This Planet and the television special The Day After have given millions of people in the Western world a horrifying picture of the effects of a nuclear conflict. No one can seriously doubt the outcome of such a war. The debate on limited nuclear war and whether a nuclear war could be won is purely theoretical. Our conclusion must be that a nuclear war cannot be won and that it would be disastrous to this planet.
Unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, the threat of nuclear war still exists, and will continue to exist as long as man knows how to manufacture nuclear arms. Technology cannot be completely eliminated. We can only attenuate its impact. And what can governments do to diminish this threat?
One of the main things Canada or any other country can do for its people is to protect them against such a threat. And the best way to do so is for the countries concerned to negotiate balanced and verifiable agreements on armament and disarmament control. Progress has been made but much remains to be done. And until this task has been accomplished, the principal guarantee for Canada's security and that of its allies must lie in a deterrence policy.
The fundamental principle of deterrence is quite simple: we must ensure that a potential aggressor knows that if he attacks us, the price he will have to pay will be so high that no conceivable objective could justify doing so. Of course this is not the ideal way to ensure one's security, but it is the only realistic approach available in the present circumstances, and it has served us well for nearly 40 years, despite the problems in East-West relations. Mr. Speaker, we must continue to support this principle while seeking a better solution.
Declaring Canada a nuclear arms free zone would do absolutely nothing to diminish the threat of nuclear war to Canadians. Does anyone really believe that Canadian cities would no longer be a target for nuclear arms if we were to declare this country a nuclear arms free zone? At the same time our withdrawal from NATO might force us to triple or quadruple our defence budget, if only to maintain our present level of security.
Although it has adopted a deterrent policy with respect to NATO, the Canadian Government has not given up its objective to reduce the nuclear arms arsenal to the lowest level possible through verifiable disarmament and arms control agreements. That is one of the major aspects of our policy on security. Canada is an active participant in the activities of the United Nations and of the Geneva disarmament conference, not to mention the Vienna discussions on mutual and balanced force reductions. As a NATO member we are also party to the organization's consultations on the nuclear forces reduction negotiations. As you know, Mr. Speaker, Canada is also
represented at the Stockholm conference on confidence and security measures and on European disarmament. As the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) stated before the United Nations last September, and 1 quote:
"-I offer Canada's encouragement and support in our quest for the climate of confidence required to conclude disarmament agreements. However frustrated we may feel, we must never fail in our determination to build a world wide security system based on a decrease rather than an increase in weaponry. If stronger political will is necessary, let us indeed show such political will, particularly on the eve of 1986 which has been proclaimed the Year of International Peace... Canada will continue playing an active role in all multilateral representations and contributing even more to restore confidence. In that respect Canada has set up an action program for the second phase of the current disarmament decade. Through this program we will double our efforts to improve the verification processes necessary to ensure compliance with the existing agreements.
Mr. Speaker, thank you for giving me this opportunity to make a statement on this issue.

subtopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE-COMPENSATION FOR SINKING OF THE LADY MARJORIE
NATIONAL DEFENCE-COMPENSATION FOR SINKING OF THE LADY MARJORIE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my purpose in rising this evening is to present to the House once again the claim of Walter Theriault in respect of the sinking of the Lady Marjorie on April 28, 1985. I think I should begin by pointing out to the House that one of the most ancient rights of Canadians is to present their case to the House of Commons. I have no hesitation-and I make no apology-in bringing to this national Chamber the case of one person who feels aggrieved under the laws of Canada and indeed by the officers of the Government of Canada.
I should explain that the incident which gave rise to Mr. Theriault's claim arose in the following way. His fishing trawler, the Lady Marjorie, was proceeding off the coast of Nova Scotia in the course of fishing and developed some difficulty. As a result of that difficulty over a period of a few days, the crew who were of a relatively young age decided to abandon the fishing trawler and at that point summoned assistance.
The vessel most readily available to provide assistance was the H.M.C.S. Nipigon, a destroyer which was part of the naval fleet of the Maritime Command. Therein the difficulty arose. I will not pretend to know the facts which transpired between the abandonment of the fishing vessel, Lady Marjorie, by its crew and the sinking which resulted from the gunfire of the H.M.C.S. Nipigon, but the end result was that the ship was a total loss; it was sunk.
One would hope and think that in this modern world, a world in which Government respects the rights and duties of individuals and of the collective society, this kind of case could be worked out in fairness to all concerned, considering the might and the power of the Government of Canada, on the one hand, and the difficulties faced by an ordinary Nova Scotia fisherman and owner of a fishing trawler, on the other hand. However, that has not been the case.
I think this is what prompted my colleague, the Hon. Member for South West Nova (Mr. Comeau), to raise the
Adjournment Debate
case in the House of Commons on May 2, 1985, when he questioned the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Nielsen) in respect of the advancement of the claim of Walter Theriault resulting from the loss of the Lady Marjorie.
At that point in time it was indicated by the Minister-and it has been repeated many times in the public press and by other media-that the sinking resulted from a decision that the Lady Marjorie constituted a hazard to navigation and had to be disposed of in the manner in which it was disposed of, that is to say, sunk.
The House of Commons plays no role in the arbitration of that kind of dispute, but it plays a role in the area of justice for all Canadians. That is what I sought by raising a question on September 25, 1985, and I do so again this evening in the House of Commons. What I seek for Mr. Walter Theriault, his family and all those involved in the operation of the fishing vessel, Lady Marjorie, is justice from the Government of Canada and from the officers of the Government of Canada.
I say this because of a report today in The Chronicle Herald of Halifax indicating that the board of inquiry, apparently commissioned to inquire into the events which led to the sinking of the Lady Marjorie, has concluded that there was no fault on the part of the Canadian Navy. Presumably that might result in a decision by the Government of Canada or the relevant Minister to deny any claim or responsibility to Walter Theriault. That would be an unfortunate decision at this point in time because Mr. Theriault faces the following difficulties. The insurers of the vessel, Lady Marjorie, say that the vessel was not in danger, could have continued afloat, and could have been salvaged. They deny any claim of the onwer, Mr. Theriault, on that ground. Apparently the advisers to the Government and the Canadian Navy indicated that the ship was about to sink, was a danger to navigation and could not be salvaged and therefore it was right and proper to carrying out its destruction by sinking and on that grounds deny any liability.
Mr. Theriault is between the proverbial rock and a hard place. On the one hand the insurers have refused payment because the ship was salvageable. On the other hand, the Canadian Government refuses assistance because the ship was a total loss.
How is this difficulty going to be worked out? I am afraid 1 do not know, but I call upon the Government to work toward some resolution, and I am not the only one to do so. On September 16, 1985, an editorial in The Daily News, a newspaper that circulates in the Halifax area, quite properly asked the question, "Will somebody please help Mr. Theriault?" I shall quote very briefly from that editorial;
Hindsight is fine in saying the Nipigon should have stood by the vessel until towing arrangements were made, and we are sure that the gunfire decision was not made lightly. But now it is clear it was made wrongly.
I do not necessarily agree with that conclusion but 1 do agree with this proposition: the Lady Marjorie has been lost to Mr. Theriault and his family and they are on the brink of
October 10, 1985

Adjournment Debate
bankruptcy as a result of the loss. Somebody should assist them, either the insurance company or the Government. I ask the Government to intervene directly and resolve this matter to the satisfaction of the Theriault family.

speakeroldname: Mr. Robert Wenman (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
subtopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE-COMPENSATION FOR SINKING OF THE LADY MARJORIE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to agree with the Hon. Member regarding his ancient right to represent the problems of his constituents in the House of Commons. 1 hope it is not only an ancient right but a present right and a continuing right for many generations to come. I would like to confirm that not only has the Hon. Member done his duty and represented his people ably in the House of Commons but in addition to that he has made very direct recommendations to all those concerned including the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Nielsen) and the Associate Minister of National Defence (Mr. Andre) in his attempt to find a resolution to this problem on behalf of his constituent.
As the Hon. Member is probably aware, the Department of National Defence, because of its concern, did set up a board of inquiry to investigate the circumstances surrounding this unfortunate incident. The Ministry of Transport has also carried out investigations which are being prepared by the Marine Casualty Investigations Branch of the Coast Guard. In so far as the Department of National Defence Board of Inquiry is concerned, the Hon. Member will be pleased to know that the inquiry has now been completed. I understand that the Ministry of Transport has yet to finalize its report but it should be made available to the public in the very near future.
The legal representative of the Lady Marjorie's owners has been in touch with DND's legal agent, the Department of Justice. I understand that intensive discussions on the subject are ongoing. I share the Hon. Member's concern that this matter be dealt with as expeditiously as possible. It is important, however, that this matter be dealt with in the most proper and deliberate way to ensure thoroughness and that justice and equity will be served. This will ensure that the important elements concerning the specific circumstances of the sinking and the legal implications are thoroughly worked out and that the appropriate action therefore follows.

subtopic: CONSUMER AFFAIRS-DISCOUNTING OF INCOME TAX REFUNDS. (B) REQUEST THAT PRACTICE BE BANNED
CONSUMER AFFAIRS-DISCOUNTING OF INCOME TAX REFUNDS. (B) REQUEST THAT PRACTICE BE BANNED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today there was a media and Member of Parliament information briefing by the National Anti-Poverty Organization with regard to income tax discounting, a practice which is growing at an alarming rate. The position of the National Anti-Poverty Organization is one which is supported by organizations as diverse as the Co-operative Association for Family Economy in Quebec, the Consumer's Association of Canada and the National Working Group on the Economy and Poverty of the United Church of Canada.
These anti-poverty, consumer and church groups want the abolition of tax discounting. They want that because they
realize that tax discounting is now permitted and encouraged by an Act passed in 1978 by the then Liberal Government. The Tax Rebate Discounting Act of 1978 was brought into effect because it was believed that with no legislation people, particularly poor peole, were paying exhorbitant rates for small amounts of money. The Act of 1978 set the maximum rate of interest which could be charged at 15 per cent. We are talking about a rate of interest which does not last for a year. It lasts for four, five or eight weeks, after which time people would receive their income tax rebate. Therefore, the actual rate of interest calculated on an annual basis is probably closer to 100 per cent than it is to the 15 per cent permitted by the Act.
We know now that almost two-thirds of those people who used the tax discount in 1984 had incomes of $8,000 or less. Yet, the same people, of whom there are now almost 400,000 were entitled to $274 million in refunds, or an average of $714 each. For a fairly simple paper work task, the tax discounters have been picking up an average of $170 for each transaction, according to the administration of the Tax Rebate Discounting Act in the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. The Department, as keeper of statistics on tax discounting, has defined the problem as being far too much of poor people's money being diverted into the hands of what are usurious lenders officially brought into being and permitted to operate by this legislation.
Since the problem is quite clear and since the people most adversely affected are people who very frequently get all or almost of their tax discount as a result of a child tax credit, it seems to us that what the Government should do is simply repeal the Act. After all, this was a Liberal Act and it was in Liberal times that organizations such as those I have mentioned started to call upon the Government to repeal the Act in order to prohibit tax discounting.
The Hon. Member who preceded me as spokesperson for the New Democratic Party on consumer and corporate affairs called on Liberal Governments to repeal the Act. Since the Liberals have been in opposition, members of their Party have called on the Government to repeal the Act. I have frequently called upon the Minister to repeal the Act.
The child tax credit system this year will deliver $367 to each person receiving that credit, a payment which will rise to $524 in 1988. By the Government's own reckoning, almost $20 million of the $41 million taken by discounters in 1984 came from the child tax credit. Why do we permit this to take place? I wonder what the Auditor General would think of this misuse of funds voted by Parliament. Far worse, how can the poorest of Canadians afford to give up this kind of money? They are forced to do it because the Government legislation permits it and the slow processing of income tax returns sees to it that they try to get their money quickly.
I ask the Government to act. We have been raising this question, as have the organizations I have mentioned, almost from the day this Government was formed. The studies which the Minister has promised have gone on almost from the time the Government took office. There were studies carried out by
October 10, 1985

the Liberal Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. If this Government can bring in legislation to pay out $1 billion to depositors of the Canadian Commercial Bank and the Northland Bank, surely it can deal with this. The Minister has promised studies. He has consulted with the provinces. I understand that the Ministers of Consumers Affairs of all the provinces have agreed that the discounting of the child tax credit, at least, should be probited. That is not all that organizations such as NAPO have been calling for, but at least that would be a beginning. I therefore say to the Minister to stop dithering, get on with the job and bring in legislation to repeal the Act which has permitted this tax discounting.
The Minister says there are problems. I say to the Minister that the Province of Quebec has prohibited tax discounting and the United States, with the most pro-business Government the country has had in 50 years, has prohibited tax discounting. I say to the Minister to stop dithering and bring in a proposal which can be passed by Parliament quickly. I ask him to bring in legislation which would prohibit income tax discounting before the next income tax year. We have had enough of studies. We have had enough of waiting. Let the Minister show some concern for the consumer. After all, he is the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Cote).

speakeroldname: Mr. Bill Domm (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and Canada Post):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subtopic: CONSUMER AFFAIRS-DISCOUNTING OF INCOME TAX REFUNDS. (B) REQUEST THAT PRACTICE BE BANNED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of the Tax Rebate Discounting Act is to protect the interest of taxpayers who give up their rights to anticipated tax refunds in order to receive immediate cash. The statute was enacted in 1978 at the urging of the provincial Governments. Prior to 1978, the discounting business was unregulated and discounters often charged rates of 40 per cent or 50 per cent of the value of the refund. The legislation now limits the legal discount rate to 15 per cent. Thus, Canadians who wish to receive immediate cash can freely choose to patronize a legitimate discounter without fear of having to pay the "loan shark" rates previously charged.
Adjournment Debate
Nevertheless, some conditions have changed significantly since 1978, and this Government must determine whether the protection given by the Tax Rebate Discounting Act is still appropriate. For that reason, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Cote) began dealing with the question early this year by initiating extensive consultation and study.
A major step in this process of consultation was the release of a discussion paper on discounting in June of this year. This paper was made available to the general public. In fact, copies were sent to all Members of Parliament. In addition, a number of interested parties were invited to respond to the Minister and to meet with him personally.
A special conference of representatives of major interested social welfare groups, discounters and business groups was held in August. The issue was on the agenda of the federal-provincial Territorial Conference of Ministers of Consumer and Corporate Affairs in September in Manitoba.
Contrary to the assertion of the Hon. Member, outlawing tax rebate discounting is not universally accepted as the solution to the problems associated with discounting. The Hon. Member surely appreciates that the discounting issue involves considerations of social policy, economic policy, federal-provincial relations and interdepartmental co-ordination. The intention of the Minister is to ensure an appropriate balance between the values represented by the market-place economy and freedom of choice, on the one hand, and the need for consumer protection on the other. This House can expect an indication soon of any adjustments which need to be made in order to maintain that balance.
In summary, the answer to the Hon. Member's question is simply that the tax rebate discount in question is being dealt with at this very moment and in the proper fashion.
